A.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
A.q: A 61-year-old man is found unresponsive and pulseless. His monitor shows this. What is the rhythm?
opts: Asystole
Asystole is a lack of electrical activity, a flat line. This strip shows continuous small chaotic waves, which is fibrillation.
Pulseless electrical activity
Pulseless electrical activity is an organized rhythm without a pulse. These waves are disorganized, with no QRS complexes.
Ventricular standstill
Ventricular standstill shows upright P waves marching across with no QRS. This strip has no P waves, only chaotic ventricular activity.
Fine ventricular fibrillation
Correct. Low-amplitude chaotic waves with no measurable P waves, QRS complexes or T waves are fine ventricular fibrillation, not a flat line.
A.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 14
A.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

A.io: Compare and contrast ECG manifestations of electrolyte abnormalities.
A.q: A 52-year-old man has the leads shown, with flattened T waves and the arrowed waves after them. Which electrolyte disturbance best explains this?
opts: Hyperkalemia
Hyperkalemia peaks the T wave; flattened T waves with prominent U waves are its opposite.
Hypercalcemia
Hypercalcemia shortens the ST segment and QTc so the T wave hugs the QRS; it does not bring out U waves.
Hypokalemia
Correct. Hypokalemia (serum potassium below 3.5 mEq/L) prolongs repolarization: T-wave flattening, prominent U waves and ST depression are its classic signs.
Hypocalcemia
Hypocalcemia lengthens the ST segment but leaves the T wave normally shaped, without prominent U waves.
A.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 37; tracing from Slide 38
A.alt: Leads V4, V5 and V6 on grid paper, with red arrows pointing to part of each beat

A.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
A.q: A 49-year-old woman is told her premature beats come in a trigeminal pattern. Which premature beats can form such patterns?
opts: All three types
Correct. Premature atrial, junctional and ventricular complexes can all come in bigeminy, trigeminy and quadrigeminy.
Ventricular only
Premature ventricular complexes do form these patterns, but so do atrial and junctional ones.
Atrial only
Atrial bigeminy and trigeminy exist, but junctional and ventricular premature beats follow the same patterns.
Escape beats only
Escape beats come late, after a pause; the patterns describe premature beats of any origin.
A.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 73

A.io: Recognize common supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation
A.q: A 66-year-old woman's rate is 65 per minute (normal 60 to 100); her strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Wandering atrial pacemaker
Correct. P waves of at least three shapes, each married to its QRS, an irregular rhythm and a rate under 100 make a wandering atrial pacemaker.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia needs a rate over 100 per minute; at 65 this is a wandering atrial pacemaker.
Premature atrial complexes
Premature atrial complexes are occasional early beats in an otherwise sinus rhythm; here the P wave shape keeps changing.
Normal sinus rhythm
Normal sinus rhythm is regular with one P wave shape; here it is irregular with several.
A.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 11, 15, 16
A.alt: Wide pink grid strip with deep narrow complexes at uneven spacing; the small waves in front of them change shape.

A.io: Topic — Thyroid disorders
A.q: A 67-year-old woman has hypothyroidism. Which tracing finding fits her condition?
opts: Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia is the commonest hyperthyroid finding, from adrenergic hyperactivity.
A shortened QTc
Hypothyroidism prolongs the QTc; a short QTc is hypercalcemia.
Low-voltage QRS
Correct. Hypothyroidism slows metabolism and contractility: sinus bradycardia with global low-voltage QRS complexes, flattened or inverted T waves, a prolonged QTc and low-amplitude P waves.
Peaked T waves
Peaked T waves are hyperkalemia; hypothyroid T waves are flattened or inverted.
A.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 44

A.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
A.q: A 36-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram. On a systematic read, how is her QRS assessed?
opts: Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block would widen the QRS to 0.12 seconds or longer with an rSR in V1. This QRS is narrow.
Within normal limits
Correct. The QRS is narrow, with no bundle branch or fascicular block pattern: within normal limits, with a normal axis and no enlargement.
Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block would widen the QRS and notch the lateral leads. This QRS is narrow.
Left anterior fascicular block
Left anterior fascicular block needs left axis deviation. This axis is normal: lead I and aVF are positive.
A.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 42
A.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

A.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
A.q: A 26-year-old man's lead V6 shows much more T wave than ST elevation. Which diagnosis does this favor?
opts: Acute pericarditis
Pericarditis has more ST elevation relative to the T wave, an ST-to-T ratio above 25% in V6.
Hypercalcemia
Hypercalcemia shortens the ST segment until the T wave sits on the QRS; it is not judged by the V6 ratio.
Early repolarization
Correct. In early repolarization there is more T wave than ST elevation in V6 (ratio under 25%); pericarditis has more ST elevation than T wave.
Type 2 Brugada
Brugada changes are confined to V1 to V3 and are not judged by the V6 ratio.
A.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 9

A.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
A.q: A 45-year-old woman notices skipped beats; her strip is shown. What are the early beats?
opts: Premature ventricular complexes
Premature ventricular complexes are wide, with no P wave and an opposite-direction T wave; these early beats are narrow with a P wave.
Premature atrial complexes
Correct. The early beats are narrow and each has its own P wave, shaped differently from the sinus P waves: premature atrial complexes.
Premature junctional complexes
A premature junctional complex has no P wave, an inverted one or one after the QRS; these early beats have an upright P of new shape.
Junctional escape beats
Escape beats come late, after a pause; these beats come early, before the next expected beat.
A.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 6, 7
A.alt: Lead II strip with narrow complexes; some beats arrive early, each with a small wave before it that differs in shape from the others.

A.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
A.q: A 77-year-old woman with a ventricular pacemaker has a T wave after each paced beat. In which direction does that T wave point?
opts: Opposite to the QRS complex
Correct. A ventricular paced beat has a contralateral T wave, one going the opposite direction of the QRS complex.
The same direction as the QRS
A T wave in the same direction as the QRS is the normal pattern of a conducted beat, not a paced ventricle.
Hidden inside the QRS
The T wave of a paced beat is separate and visible after the wide QRS, pointing the opposite way.
Absent after every paced beat
Paced ventricular beats repolarize, so a T wave follows each one. It points opposite to the QRS.
A.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 18

A.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
A.q: A 70-year-old woman has a bundle branch block. Which lead decides whether the block is right or left?
opts: Lead II
Lead II is the rhythm lead; the side of a bundle branch block is read in V1, by the first deflection before the J point.
aVR
aVR does not decide the side of the block; V1 does, through the direction of the deflection just before the J point.
V4
V4 does not decide the side; V1 decides it, and V6 is where the double QRS phenomenon is best seen.
V1
Correct. Find the J point in V1 and travel backward: if the first deflection you reach is positive the block is right-sided, and if it is negative the block is left-sided.
A.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 16

A.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
A.q: A 69-year-old woman's strip is shown. How is its regularity best described?
opts: Irregular
Correct. The R to R intervals differ from beat to beat (the gaps between consecutive complexes are visibly unequal), so the rhythm is irregular.
Regular
A regular rhythm has the same R to R interval every beat; here consecutive gaps clearly differ.
Regular with one pause
One isolated gap in an otherwise even strip would suggest a dropped cycle; here the R to R intervals vary throughout.
Regular but slow
Slow describes the rate, not regularity; the R to R intervals here are unequal, so it is irregular.
A.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 54, 56
A.alt: Rhythm strip with narrow complexes whose spacing varies noticeably from one beat to the next.

A.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular escape rhythms
A.q: A 77-year-old man's strip shows a narrow junctional beat. How does a junctional escape beat differ in timing from a premature junctional complex?
opts: It comes early, before the next R
Arriving early defines the premature junctional complex; the escape beat comes late.
It falls every other beat
Every other beat describes bigeminy, a pattern of premature beats; an escape beat follows a pause.
It lands on the T wave
A beat on the T wave is the R on T danger of a premature ventricular complex; escape beats come late.
It comes late, after a pause
Correct. A junctional escape beat comes late, past where the next R wave was expected; a premature junctional complex comes early.
A.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 50, 52

A.io: Recognize sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia
A.q: A healthy 9-year-old boy has this strip at a routine visit. What is the rhythm?
opts: Normal sinus rhythm
Normal sinus rhythm is regular; here the R to R intervals lengthen and shorten.
Sinus exit block
Sinus exit block drops a whole cycle, leaving one gap that marches out; here intervals vary gradually.
Sinus arrhythmia
Correct. Every complex has a normal P wave married to a narrow QRS with a normal PR, but the R to R intervals vary: sinus arrhythmia, a benign finding most common in children.
Sinus pause
A sinus pause is a single sudden gap; here the spacing shifts gradually across the strip.
A.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 81, 82, 84
A.alt: Rhythm strip with three-second tick marks and narrow complexes, each preceded by a small upright wave, with gaps that vary in length.

A.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of AV nodal and infranodal conduction abnormalities
A.q: A 78-year-old woman's third-degree block has narrow QRS complexes on this strip. Where is her ventricular escape most likely coming from?
opts: The atrioventricular junction
Correct. In third-degree block the QRS is narrow or wide depending on the origin; a narrow escape comes from the atrioventricular junction, above the bundle branches.
The Purkinje and bundle-branch fibers
An escape from the Purkinje or bundle-branch fibers spreads outside the normal pathway and is wide. These complexes are narrow.
The sinoatrial node
The sinoatrial node drives only the atria in complete block. Its impulses never reach the ventricles.
Many ventricular foci
Many foci firing at once is ventricular fibrillation. A complete block has one regular escape rhythm.
A.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 48
A.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

A.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement: left atrial enlargement, right atrial enlargement
A.q: A 59-year-old woman with pulmonary hypertension has this lead II strip. Her P waves are taller than 2.5 millimeters (normal 2.5 or less). What do they indicate?
opts: Left atrial enlargement
Left atrial enlargement widens and notches the P wave rather than making it tall and peaked.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS finding in V1 and V2, not a P wave height in lead II.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy raises QRS voltage; it does not make the P wave tall.
Right atrial enlargement
Correct. An upright limb-lead P wave taller than 2.5 millimeters is P pulmonale, and one lead is enough to confirm right atrial enlargement.
A.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 29
A.alt: Single-lead tracing on electrocardiogram paper

A.io: Interpret electrocardiographic findings for sinus rhythms: sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
A.q: A 64-year-old man's strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Sinus exit block
In exit block the gap is a whole multiple of the P to P interval; this gap is about one and a half cycles, because the node reset.
Sinus pause
Correct. The node stops firing and starts again, and the next beat does not fall on the marched-out schedule, because the cycle has reset: a sinus pause.
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia is evenly slow throughout; here a steady rhythm is broken by one long gap.
Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus arrhythmia changes the spacing gradually with breathing; this is one sudden flat gap.
A.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 91
A.alt: Line drawing of a rhythm strip without grid: five narrow complexes with small upright waves before them; one longer flat stretch separates the second and third beats.

A.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: Benign Early Repolarization (BER), acute pericarditis, long QT syndrome
A.q: A 29-year-old woman has the 12-lead shown, with global concave ST elevation. Which finding in lead aVR supports pericarditis?
opts: PR-segment elevation
Correct. Pericarditis inflames the atria too, so the PR segment is depressed in most leads and elevated in aVR, alongside global concave ST elevation.
ST-segment elevation
aVR is one of the two leads where pericarditis may show ST depression; elevation in aVR is not its sign.
A pathologic Q wave
Q waves anywhere on the tracing argue against pericarditis and mean an acute infarction must be considered.
A delta wave
A delta wave is the slurred QRS upstroke of preexcitation; it has nothing to do with pericardial inflammation.
A.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 6
A.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

A.io: Discuss related anatomy and physiology of ventricular conduction abnormalities and chamber enlargement
A.q: A 66-year-old woman has ventricular hypertrophy. What does that term refer to?
opts: Stretching that dilates a chamber
Stretching and dilation is chamber enlargement, most often of the atria. Hypertrophy thickens the muscle.
Thickening that shrinks a chamber
Correct. Ventricular hypertrophy is actual enlargement and thickening of the cardiac muscle, which in turn makes the ventricular chamber smaller.
A block in a bundle branch
A bundle branch block is a conduction problem, not a change in the muscle's thickness.
Thinning that enlarges a chamber
Hypertrophy thickens the wall rather than thinning it, and the chamber becomes smaller.
A.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 32

A.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
A.q: A 66-year-old man's lead II strip is shown; his P waves are inverted. Why?
opts: The sinus node fires early
An early sinus beat keeps an upright P in lead II; inversion means the atria are activated from below.
The atria depolarize from below
Correct. A junctional impulse travels up into the atria and depolarizes them from the bottom up, away from positive lead II, so the P waves are inverted.
The ventricles fire first
Ventricles depolarizing first put the P wave after the QRS; inversion itself comes from bottom-up atrial activation.
Flutter waves replace them
Flutter waves form a continuous sawtooth; these are single inverted P waves from a junctional impulse.
A.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 47
A.alt: Lead II strip of regularly spaced narrow complexes, each preceded closely by a small downward deflection, one drawn in red.

A.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
A.q: A 26-year-old man with an accessory pathway develops a sustained reentrant tachycardia. What typically starts it?
opts: A premature beat near the pathway
Correct. A premature atrial or ventricular complex occurring near the accessory pathway can initiate premature depolarization, and the pathway plus the normal pathway form a reentry circuit.
Sudden cooling below 32 degrees Celsius
Cooling below 32 degrees Celsius produces Osborn waves; it is not the trigger of accessory pathway reentry.
A rise in serum calcium
High calcium shortens the ST segment; it is not what starts accessory pathway reentry.
Inflammation of the pericardium
Pericarditis produces global concave ST elevation, not reentrant tachycardia.
A.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 30

A.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: myocardial ischemia, myocardial injury, myocardial infarction
A.q: A 48-year-old man has had 20 minutes of chest pressure. His precordial leads are shown, with no ST elevation. What are these T waves?
opts: Normal T waves
Normal T waves are asymmetrical, with a slow initial upstroke and a sharper terminal downstroke, and their amplitude is modest. These are tall and symmetrical.
Inverted T waves
These T waves point upward. T-wave inversion is a later ischemic sign than hyperacute T waves.
Flattened T waves
Flattened T waves (a hypokalemia and hypothyroidism finding) are low and shallow; these are tall and upright.
Hyperacute T waves
Correct. Tall, increased in amplitude and symmetrical, with no ST elevation yet: hyperacute T waves, often the very first sign of cardiac ischemia.
A.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 7
A.alt: Six precordial leads, V1 to V6, on grid paper

A.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, hypocalcemia
A.q: A 68-year-old woman has hyperkalemia. Besides its classic signs, which other changes can it produce?
opts: Delta waves and a short PR
Delta waves with a short PR come from an accessory pathway, not from potassium.
Blocks and ST elevation
Correct. Hyperkalemia can cause a host of changes, such as bradycardias, tachycardias, ST elevation, T-wave abnormalities and atrioventricular and bundle branch blocks.
Osborn waves only
Osborn waves are the terminal notches of hypothermia and early repolarization.
No other changes at all
Hyperkalemia is notable for producing many different changes beyond its classic signs.
A.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 34

A.io: Compare and contrast sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
A.q: A 74-year-old man is evaluated for sick sinus syndrome. Which finding defines the condition?
opts: A single long pause
One isolated pause is a sinus pause; sick sinus syndrome is exit block, pause and arrest together.
All three on the same patient
Correct. Sick sinus syndrome is defined by sinus exit block, sinus pause and sinus arrest occurring together in one patient, often on one strip.
A rate under 60 per minute
A slow regular sinus rhythm is sinus bradycardia; sick sinus syndrome is the mixture of exit block, pause and arrest.
Variation with breathing
Breathing-related variation is sinus arrhythmia, which is benign; sick sinus syndrome is the three failures together.
A.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 101

A.io: Review ECG lead placement
A.q: A 29-year-old woman's leads I, II and III form Einthoven's triangle. Why are they called bipolar leads?
opts: Each needs two physical poles
Correct. Leads I, II and III need physical positive and negative poles on the patient, so they are the bipolar leads.
They use a central terminal
A theoretical central terminal as the negative pole is what makes the augmented and chest leads unipolar.
They view the heart horizontally
The horizontal view comes from the precordial leads; the limb leads are bipolar because of their two physical poles.
The machine creates them
The machine creates the augmented leads from one physical lead; the bipolar leads each use two physical electrodes.
A.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 62

A.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block, third-degree AV block
A.q: A 70-year-old man's PR intervals just before and just after a dropped beat are the same duration. Which block is this?
opts: Second-degree type I
Type I shows PR intervals of different duration around the dropped beat: longest before it, reset after it.
Third-degree block
Third-degree block has no PR relationship at all; the P waves are unrelated to the QRS complexes.
First-degree block
First-degree block conducts every P wave and never drops a beat, so there is no dropped beat to measure around.
Second-degree type II
Correct. If the PR intervals before and after the dropped beat are equal in duration, it is always second-degree type II.
A.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 50

A.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
A.q: A 50-year-old woman's ventricular cell is in phase 3, rapid repolarization. Which ion movement returns it to its resting voltage?
opts: Potassium entering the cell
Moving positive potassium inward would make the inside more positive, not less; repolarization is potassium flowing out of the cell.
Calcium entering the cell
Calcium channels close in phase 3; calcium entry is the phase 2 plateau that causes contraction.
Potassium leaving the cell
Correct. Calcium channels close and potassium flows out of the cell, which makes the inside negative again; potassium efflux is what repolarizes the cell.
Sodium entering the cell
Sodium influx is the phase 0 upstroke; in phase 3 the cell repolarizes as potassium leaves it.
A.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 17, 22

A.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement: left atrial enlargement, right atrial enlargement
A.q: A 70-year-old man has this lead II strip. Which chamber finding do its P waves show?
opts: Left atrial enlargement
Correct. The P waves are wide and humped with the humps well apart: P mitrale, left atrial enlargement.
Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement gives tall, peaked P waves. These are wide and double-humped.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is read from the QRS in V1 and V2. The finding here is the P wave.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS voltage finding. The finding here is the P wave.
A.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 31
A.alt: Single-lead tracing on electrocardiogram paper

A.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
A.q: A 72-year-old man's strip is shown, with a short run of consecutive wide beats. What does the run represent?
opts: A ventricular couplet
A couplet is only two premature ventricular complexes in a row; this run is six wide beats long.
Ventricular bigeminy
Bigeminy alternates single wide beats with normal ones; here the wide beats run back to back.
Ventricular tachycardia
Correct. Three or more consecutive premature ventricular complexes at a fast rate are ventricular tachycardia; a brief run like this one is nonsustained and needs evaluation.
Idioventricular rhythm
Idioventricular rhythm is a slow escape rhythm of 20 to 40 per minute; this is a fast run of ectopic beats.
A.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 70, 71
A.alt: Strip with a few narrow beats, one broad beat, then a rapid run of six broad complexes before narrow beats return.

A.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
A.q: A 57-year-old man known to have a prolonged QT interval becomes unresponsive. His monitor shows this. What is the rhythm?
opts: Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
The monomorphic form keeps one complex shape and a regular rhythm. Here the shape and amplitude keep changing.
Torsades de pointes
Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia twisting around the baseline, in a patient with a prolonged QT interval, is torsades de pointes.
Fine ventricular fibrillation
Fine ventricular fibrillation is low-amplitude chaotic squiggles with no measurable complexes. These complexes are large and wide.
Asystole
Asystole is a flat line with no electrical activity. This strip shows continuous, rapid ventricular activity.
A.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 11
A.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

A.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
A.q: A 52-year-old woman's sinoatrial impulse must reach her left atrium. Which structure is the main route?
opts: Bundle of His
The bundle of His connects the atrioventricular node to the bundle branches; atrium-to-atrium conduction runs through Bachmann's bundle.
Left bundle branch
The left bundle branch enters the left ventricle, not the left atrium; Bachmann's bundle links the two atria.
Inferior posterior tract
The inferior posterior tract is an internodal pathway toward the atrioventricular node; Bachmann's bundle reaches the left atrium.
Bachmann's bundle
Correct. Bachmann's bundle extends from the right to the left atrium and is the main route of interatrial conduction.
A.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 8

A.topic: Left bundle branch block and pacing
A.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
A.q: A 70-year-old man with chest pain has a left bundle branch block, shown here. Why is an ST-elevation infarction hard to locate on this tracing?
opts: The block hides all ST segments
The ST segments are still visible; the problem is that the block itself distorts them globally.
Wide QRS with global ST and T changes
Correct. Left bundle branch blocks and ventricular paced rhythms cause wide QRS complexes with global ST elevation and T-wave changes, which make an ST-elevation infarction difficult to locate.
Bundle branch blocks prevent infarction
A block does not protect the heart; it only makes an infarction harder to see.
The heart rate is always too fast
The difficulty is the widened, distorted ventricular complex, not the rate.
A.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 13; tracing from Slide 15
A.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

A.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
A.q: A 74-year-old man's lead II strip is shown, with the PR intervals bracketed. What is the PR interval doing?
opts: Constant across the strip
A constant PR would measure the same at every bracket; here each is longer than the last until a QRS drops.
Shortening before each beat
The brackets get wider, not narrower, until a P wave is left with no QRS.
Varying at random
The change is progressive, each PR longer than the last, ending in a dropped QRS, not random variation.
Lengthening until a beat drops
Correct. Each PR interval is longer than the one before until a P wave stands alone without a QRS; the PR interval is not constant across the strip.
A.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 59
A.alt: Lead II strip with brackets under the PR intervals of successive beats and one P wave labeled on its own.

A.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
A.q: A 63-year-old woman has an anteroseptal infarction. Which leads make up the anteroseptal territory?
opts: V1, V2, V3 and V4
Correct. The anteroseptal territory is V1 to V4: the septal leads V1 and V2 plus the anterior leads V3 and V4, with no reciprocal leads.
V3, V4, V5 and V6
V5 and V6 are lateral leads; the anteroseptal territory is V1 to V4.
II, III and aVF
II, III and aVF are the inferior leads, viewing the bottom of the left ventricle, not the septum.
I, aVL, V5 and V6
I, aVL, V5 and V6 are the lateral leads, the circumflex territory, not the anteroseptal one.
A.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 15

A.io: Recognize common supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation
A.q: A 68-year-old man's strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation has a chaotic, shapeless baseline and an irregularly irregular rhythm; this baseline is an organized sawtooth.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia shows separate P waves of three shapes; here the baseline is a repeating sawtooth.
Atrial flutter
Correct. The baseline between the narrow QRS complexes is a continuous sawtooth of flutter waves, a pattern pathognomonic of atrial flutter.
Wandering atrial pacemaker
A wandering atrial pacemaker shows distinct P waves of several shapes under 100 per minute, not a sawtooth.
A.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 24, 26, 27
A.alt: Rhythm strip with three-second tick marks: narrow complexes separated by a continuous zigzag baseline of repeating pointed waves.

A.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
A.q: A 51-year-old woman's rate is 120 per minute (normal 60 to 100); her lead II strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia shows upright P waves in lead II; inverted P waves with a short PR are junctional.
Junctional escape rhythm
A junctional escape rhythm is 40 to 60 per minute; at 120 it is junctional tachycardia.
Atrial flutter
Atrial flutter replaces P waves with a sawtooth baseline; here each QRS has a single inverted P.
Junctional tachycardia
Correct. Inverted P waves just before narrow QRS complexes, a short PR and a regular rate of 120 make junctional tachycardia (over 100).
A.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 64, 67, 68
A.alt: Lead II strip with closely spaced narrow complexes, each with a small downward deflection just before it.

A.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
A.q: A 70-year-old man's monitor shows regular, wide complexes with no P waves. Which rate range defines this rhythm?
opts: 300 to 500 per minute
That is the rate of ventricular fibrillation, which is irregular and has no measurable QRS. Ventricular tachycardia runs at 100 to 300.
20 to 40 per minute
A ventricular rate of 20 to 40 belongs to a slow escape rhythm, not a tachycardia. Ventricular tachycardia runs at 100 to 300 per minute.
100 to 300 per minute
Correct. Ventricular tachycardia runs at 100 to 300 per minute, regular, with wide QRS complexes and no P waves.
60 to 100 per minute
That is a normal rate. Ventricular tachycardia is, by name, a tachycardia, at 100 to 300 per minute.
A.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 6

A.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: left ventricular hypertrophy, right ventricular hypertrophy
A.q: A 23-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram. Which finding does it show?
opts: Right ventricular hypertrophy
Correct. Tall R waves exceeding the S waves in V1 and V2, with right axis deviation (lead I negative): right ventricular hypertrophy.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy puts deep S waves in V1 and V2 and causes left axis deviation. Here V1 is dominantly positive.
Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block makes V1 end negative with a wide QRS. V1 here is a tall positive complex.
Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement is a P wave finding. The main change on this tracing is the tall R wave in V1.
A.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 35
A.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

A.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: COPD/COLD, pulmonary embolism, hypothermia
A.q: A 50-year-old woman has sudden severe shortness of breath with clear, equal lung sounds. Her 12-lead is shown. Which pattern on it is associated with pulmonary embolism?
opts: Coved elevation in V1 to V3
Coved elevation confined to V1 to V3 is type 1 Brugada, not pulmonary embolism.
A delta wave
A delta wave marks preexcitation through an accessory pathway.
Peaked T waves
Peaked, symmetric T waves are the early sign of hyperkalemia.
S1Q3T3
Correct. A deep S wave in lead I, a Q wave in lead III and an inverted T wave in lead III, the S1Q3T3 pattern, is the classic pulmonary embolism finding, with sinus tachycardia.
A.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 50
A.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

A.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
A.q: A 61-year-old man with chest pain has ST elevation in II, III and aVF. Which criterion defines an ST-elevation myocardial infarction in these leads?
opts: 1 mm or more in two contiguous leads

Correct. An ST-elevation infarction is considered when there is 1 mm or more of elevation in 2 or more contiguous leads, with or without reciprocal changes. (Leads V2 and V3 carry higher, sex- and age-specific thresholds.)
1 mm in any single lead
One lead is not enough; the elevation must appear in two or more contiguous leads looking at the same region.
2 mm in three unrelated leads
Leads must be contiguous (same region). Elevation scattered across unrelated walls does not meet the criterion.
Any elevation with reciprocal changes
Reciprocal changes confirm but are not required; the criterion is at least 1 mm in two or more contiguous leads.
A.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 16

A.io: Define: normal axis, left axis deviation, right axis deviation
A.q: A 40-year-old man's electrocardiogram is reviewed for axis. Which range is the normal electrical axis?
opts: 0 to +180 degrees
That range would take in most of right axis deviation. The normal axis runs from -30 to +90 degrees.
-30 to +90 degrees
Correct. The normal electrical axis ranges between -30 and +90 degrees; both lead I and aVF are mostly positive.
+90 to +180 degrees
That is right axis deviation, where lead I turns negative and aVF stays positive.
-30 to -90 degrees
That is left axis deviation, where lead I is positive and aVF negative.
A.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 20

A.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: incomplete and complete right bundle branch block, incomplete and complete left bundle branch block
A.q: A 77-year-old woman has a wide QRS with slurred S waves in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6. Which block is this?
opts: Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block notches the lateral QRS complexes and removes their Q waves; it does not give slurred S waves.
Left anterior fascicular block
A fascicular block keeps the QRS narrow and is diagnosed by axis and limb-lead patterns.
Right bundle branch block
Correct. Slurred S waves in the lateral leads are a right bundle branch block criterion, the double QRS phenomenon best seen in V6.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy gives tall lateral R waves with a normal duration, not slurred S waves.
A.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 16

A.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
A.q: A 19-year-old man has occasional palpitations. His 12-lead in sinus rhythm is shown. Which pattern does it show?
opts: Left bundle branch block
A bundle branch block widens the QRS but leaves the PR interval normal and has no delta wave.
Ventricular paced rhythm
A paced rhythm has a pacing spike before each wide QRS, not a short PR interval with a slurred delta wave.
Brugada syndrome
Brugada changes are coved or saddleback ST elevation in V1 to V3, not a short PR with a delta wave.
Wolff-Parkinson-White
Correct. A short PR interval, a slurred upstroke of the QRS (delta wave) and a widened QRS, the diagnostic triad, is Wolff-Parkinson-White preexcitation.
A.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 28
A.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

A.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block Type I, second-degree AV block Type II, third-degree AV block
A.q: A 34-year-old woman feels well. Her PR interval is longer than 0.20 seconds (normal 0.12 to 0.20) on this strip. What is the rhythm?
opts: First-degree atrioventricular block
Correct. A sinus rhythm with every P wave conducted and a PR interval beyond 0.2 seconds is first-degree atrioventricular block.
Second-degree type I (Wenckebach)
Type I shows a PR that lengthens until a P wave is not conducted. On this strip every P wave is followed by a QRS.
Second-degree type II (Mobitz II)
Type II drops QRS complexes after some P waves. Nothing is dropped on this strip.
Third-degree (complete) block
Third-degree block shows P waves unrelated to the QRS. Here each P wave is married to the QRS that follows it.
A.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 26
A.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

A.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
A.q: A 66-year-old woman has chest pressure at rest. Her 12-lead is shown. Which finding is present across most leads?
opts: ST-segment depression
Correct. The J point and ST segment sit below the baseline in nearly every lead. Global ST-segment depression is the picture of subendocardial ischemia.
ST-segment elevation
ST elevation would put the J point above the baseline in contiguous leads; here it sits below it almost everywhere, which is depression.
Pathologic Q waves
Pathologic Q waves are deep, wide initial negative deflections that mark dead tissue. These complexes begin with normal upstrokes; the change is in the ST segment.
Hyperacute T waves
Hyperacute T waves are broad, tall and symmetrical. The abnormality on this tracing is the ST segment dropping below baseline, not an enlarged T wave.
A.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 9
A.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

A.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
A.q: A 33-year-old man's monitor prints this six-second strip. What is his ventricular rate?
opts: 130 per minute
Correct. Thirteen QRS complexes fall in the six seconds, and thirteen times ten is 130 per minute.
110 per minute
One hundred ten would be eleven complexes in six seconds; there are thirteen here, giving 130.
150 per minute
One hundred fifty would need fifteen complexes; thirteen times ten is 130 per minute.
65 per minute
Sixty-five halves the count; the six-second method multiplies thirteen complexes by ten, giving 130.
A.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 44, 47
A.alt: Six-second rhythm strip with tick marks at the start, middle and end, and regularly spaced narrow complexes.

A.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
A.q: A 58-year-old man's 12-lead is shown, with ST elevation in II, III and aVF. How should the ST depression in leads I and aVL be read?
opts: As a second infarction
Reciprocal depression is the mirror image of one event seen from the opposite side, not evidence of a separate infarction.
As lateral subendocardial ischemia
With ST elevation on the same tracing, depression is read as reciprocal first. Global depression without elevation is what points to subendocardial ischemia.
As a lead placement error
Mirror-image depression in the leads opposite an infarct is expected physiology, and it is a confirmatory sign of ischemia, not a technical fault.
As a reciprocal change
Correct. ST depression should always be considered a reciprocal change when ST elevation exists in the same tracing. I and aVL mirror the inferior leads, and the depression confirms the event.
A.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 14; tracing from Slide 16
A.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

A.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block, third-degree AV block
A.q: A 60-year-old woman's strip shows a dropped beat. How does the PR interval after the dropped beat compare with the one before it?
opts: It is the same
Equal PR intervals before and after the dropped beat would make this second-degree type II. Here the PR resets shorter.
It is longer
The PR is longest just before the dropped beat. After the drop it resets to its shortest.
It is shorter
Correct. After the dropped beat the cycle begins over, so the next PR is shorter than the last, longest PR before the drop: second-degree type I.
It cannot be measured
The P wave after the dropped beat is conducted, so its PR can be measured; it is shorter than the one before the drop.
A.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 50
A.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

A.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: digoxin toxicity, amiodarone toxicity, tricyclic antidepressant toxicity
A.q: A 23-year-old woman took an overdose of amitriptyline, a tricyclic antidepressant. Her 12-lead is shown. Which drug effect causes her fast heart rate?
opts: Beta-receptor blockade
Beta blockade slows the heart; it is one of amiodarone's actions, not the cause of tricyclic tachycardia.
Anticholinergic activity
Correct. Tricyclic antidepressants' anticholinergic activity causes the tachycardia; their fast sodium-channel blockade widens the QRS (the wide complexes on this tracing), and the QT is prolonged.
Sodium-potassium pump inhibition
Pump inhibition is digoxin's mechanism, with frequent premature ventricular complexes as its commonest result.
Raised serum calcium
High calcium shortens the ST segment and QTc; it is not what speeds the heart in a tricyclic overdose.
A.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 49
A.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

A.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
A.q: A 66-year-old woman has ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6. Which region does this localize to?
opts: Inferior wall
The inferior wall is viewed by II, III and aVF, which are the reciprocal leads of a lateral infarction.
Lateral wall
Correct. I, aVL, V5 and V6 are the lateral leads, and the lateral wall's reciprocal leads are II, III and aVF.
Anteroseptal wall
The anteroseptal wall is viewed by V1 to V4; elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6 is lateral.
Posterior wall
The posterior wall has no facing lead on the standard 12-lead; its reciprocal leads are V1 to V4.
A.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 15

A.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
A.q: A 61-year-old man's 12-lead is shown, with ST elevation in I and aVL and reciprocal depression in III and aVF. Occlusion of which artery best explains it?
opts: Right coronary artery
The right coronary artery supplies the right heart and the bottom of the left ventricle; its occlusion elevates II, III and aVF, which are depressed here.
A coronary vein
The coronary veins return used blood to the right atrium; an infarction pattern comes from an arterial occlusion.
Left circumflex artery

Correct. The circumflex wraps around to supply the left atrium and the side and back of the left ventricle, so of these arteries it best explains a lateral infarction (a diagonal branch of the left anterior descending can also cause one).
Left main coronary artery
A left main occlusion starves both of its branches, so the anterior and septal leads would be elevated too, not the high lateral leads alone.
A.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 4; tracing from Slide 17
A.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

A.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
A.q: A 44-year-old woman asks what the letter J in J point stands for. What does it stand for?
opts: Joint
It is not a joint; the J point is the junction where the QRS complex ends and the ST segment begins.
Jump
Nothing jumps there; J stands for junction, the meeting point of the QRS and the ST segment.
Jugular
Jugular refers to the neck veins (jugular vein distension is a right ventricular sign); J point means junction point.
Junction
Correct. The junction point, or J point, is the junction between the QRS complex and the ST segment.
A.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 5

A.io: Correlate ECG findings with clinical implications of ventricular arrhythmias and AV blocks
A.q: A 58-year-old woman is unresponsive, and her monitor shows this organized rhythm. Which finding would make it pulseless electrical activity?
opts: Absent P waves
This rhythm has a P wave before each QRS, and pulseless electrical activity can look like any organized rhythm. The pulse decides it.
An irregular rhythm
Regularity does not define it; pulseless electrical activity can be any organized rhythm. Only the missing pulse does.
No palpable pulse
Correct. Pulseless electrical activity can look like any organized rhythm, even normal sinus; it is the absence of a pulse that makes the diagnosis.
Inverted T waves
T wave direction does not make the diagnosis. Organized electrical activity becomes pulseless electrical activity when there is no pulse.
A.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 16
A.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

A.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, SVT, atrial tachycardia
A.q: A 70-year-old woman's strip shows no P waves in atrial fibrillation. What replaces them?
opts: Flutter waves
Flutter waves form the organized sawtooth of atrial flutter; fibrillation shows disorganized fibrillatory waves.
Inverted P waves
Inverted P waves come from a junctional impulse; fibrillation has fibrillatory waves instead of P waves.
Retrograde P waves
Retrograde P waves follow the QRS in junctional beats and reentry tachycardia; fibrillation shows fibrillatory waves.
Fibrillatory waves
Correct. Atrial fibrillation has no P waves; fibrillatory (f) waves are present instead, and the atrial rate is indeterminate.
A.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 33, 35, 37

A.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction.
A.q: A 64-year-old woman's chart says she has transmural ischemia. Which other term refers to the same thing?
opts: Subendocardial ischemia
Subendocardial ischemia is confined to the inner layer and shows as ST depression; transmural ischemia spans the full wall.
Myocardial injury
Correct. Transmural ischemia is also referred to as injury, and it is represented on the tracing by ST-segment elevation.
Pathologic Q wave formation
Pathologic Q waves mark infarction, the death of tissue; transmural ischemia is injury, which shows as ST elevation.
Early repolarization
Early repolarization is a benign normal variant of ST elevation, not a synonym for transmural ischemia.
A.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 10

A.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of supraventricular arrhythmias
A.q: A 26-year-old woman's strip is shown; her rate jumps abruptly from about 100 to about 200 per minute (normal 60 to 100). What kind of beat usually sets off this reentry tachycardia?
opts: A ventricular escape beat
An escape beat arrives late after nodal failure; the reentry tachycardia is usually started by an early atrial ectopic beat.
A dropped sinus cycle
A dropped cycle is sinus exit block; a narrow-complex reentry tachycardia usually starts with a premature atrial complex.
A premature atrial complex
Correct. Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia is usually set off by an ectopic beat, typically a premature atrial complex near the fast or slow tract.
A junctional escape beat
Junctional escape beats come late after the sinus node fails; the usual trigger is an early atrial beat.
A.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 38
A.alt: Pink grid strip labeled 100 bpm on the left and 200 bpm on the right; regular narrow complexes abruptly become twice as frequent.

A.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ventricular hypertrophy
A.q: A 64-year-old woman has ST elevation that may not be an infarction. Which condition is the most common mimic of ST-elevation infarction?
opts: Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is not on the list of infarction mimics; left ventricular hypertrophy is the most common mimic.
Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement is a P wave finding and does not mimic ST elevation.
Left anterior fascicular block
A fascicular block shifts the axis; it is not on the list of infarction mimics.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Correct. Left ventricular hypertrophy is known as the most common mimic of ST-elevation myocardial infarction: it alters repolarization, changing the ST segment and T wave.
A.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 58

A.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes
A.q: A 74-year-old woman is in cardiac arrest. Which finding defines ventricular standstill?
opts: QRS complexes with no P waves
QRS complexes without P waves describe a ventricular rhythm such as ventricular tachycardia. Standstill has P waves and no QRS.
P waves with no QRS complexes
Correct. In ventricular standstill there are atrial contractions but no ventricular contractions: obvious upright P waves march out with no QRS.
A flat line with no waves
A flat line is asystole. Ventricular standstill keeps its P waves.
Chaotic waves with no QRS
Chaotic waves without measurable complexes are ventricular fibrillation. Standstill has orderly P waves.
A.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 17

A.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
A.q: A 63-year-old man has this electrocardiogram. What is his electrical axis?
opts: Normal axis
A normal axis has a mostly positive QRS in both lead I and aVF; the normal range is -30 to +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation has lead I mostly negative and aVF mostly positive, an axis beyond +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Left axis deviation
Correct. Lead I is mostly positive and aVF is mostly negative: left axis deviation.
Extreme axis deviation
Extreme axis deviation, no man's land, has both lead I and aVF mostly negative. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
A.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 24
A.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

A.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of sinus node dysfunction
A.q: A 75-year-old woman's strip shows sinus exit block. What is her sinoatrial node doing during the missing cycle?
opts: Not firing at all
A node that stops firing and restarts is a sinus pause or arrest; in exit block it fires but the impulse is blocked.
Firing, but blocked
Correct. In sinus exit block the sinus node fires as normal, but the impulse is blocked from leaving it, so a cardiac cycle is absent.
Resetting its own timing
Resetting is what makes a sinus pause; in exit block the node keeps its timing, so beats march out.
Firing faster than normal
Faster firing would raise the rate; in exit block the node fires normally but the impulse does not exit.
A.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 85
A.alt: Monitor strip with narrow complexes and the gaps labeled underneath in seconds: 1.1, 1.0, 2.2 and 1.0.

A.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
A.q: A 51-year-old woman is told her blocked artery supplies the front of the left ventricle and the front of the septum. Which artery is it?
opts: Right coronary artery
The right coronary artery supplies the back of the septum, the right heart and the bottom of the left ventricle, not the front of the septum.
Left circumflex artery
The circumflex runs around to the side and back of the left ventricle; it does not supply the front of the septum.
Left anterior descending
Correct. The left anterior descending artery supplies the front (and bottom) of the left ventricle and the front of the septum, which is why it carries septal and anterior infarctions.
Coronary veins
The coronary veins return oxygen-poor blood to the right atrium. Arteries, here the left anterior descending, supply the muscle.
A.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 4

B.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
B.q: A 74-year-old woman has frequent, grouped premature ventricular complexes. What can they do to her circulation?
opts: Raise cardiac output
Early ventricular beats come before the ventricles fill; frequent or grouped ones reduce output.
Reduce cardiac output
Correct. Frequent premature ventricular complexes, especially grouped ones, can cause a reduction in cardiac output.
Leave output unchanged
Isolated ones may be harmless, but frequent or grouped premature ventricular complexes reduce cardiac output.
Improve atrial filling
Ectopic ventricular beats do nothing for atrial filling; frequent ones reduce cardiac output.
B.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 70

B.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: digoxin toxicity, amiodarone toxicity, tricyclic antidepressant toxicity
B.q: A 69-year-old woman on amiodarone has a prolonged QT. Which effect of the drug explains it?
opts: It shortens phase 2
Shortening phase 2 would shorten the ST segment and QT, as hypercalcemia does.
It slows phase 3
Correct. Amiodarone slows phase 3 of the cardiac action potential, causing QT prolongation; it also suppresses sinoatrial automaticity and slows atrioventricular conduction.
It speeds phase 0
Amiodarone reduces conduction velocity; it does not speed the sodium upstroke.
It adds a delta wave
A delta wave comes from an accessory pathway, not from a drug.
B.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 48

B.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of myocardial ischemia and infarction.
B.q: A 59-year-old man has ST-segment elevation from transmural ischemia. Through which part of the wall does the ischemia extend?
opts: The innermost layer only
Ischemia confined to the innermost layer is subendocardial ischemia, which shows as ST depression.
The outer epicardium only
The epicardium lies next to the coronary arteries; transmural means across the whole wall, not one layer.
The full wall thickness
Correct. Transmural ischemia spans the full thickness of the wall (it is also called injury) and is represented by ST elevation.
The pericardial sac
The pericardium is outside the myocardium; its inflammation is pericarditis, not transmural ischemia.
B.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 10

B.io: Recognize common supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation
B.q: A 60-year-old man's rate is 60 per minute (normal 60 to 100); his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Wandering atrial pacemaker
Correct. The rhythm is irregular, under 100 per minute, with P waves of at least three different shapes still married to the QRS: a wandering atrial pacemaker.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia has the same three-shape P waves but runs over 100 per minute; at 60 it is a wandering atrial pacemaker.
Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus arrhythmia is irregular too, but every P wave has the same sinus shape; here the P waves change shape.
Atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation has no P waves at all, only fibrillatory waves; here distinct P waves precede every QRS.
B.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 11, 12, 13, 14
B.alt: Pink grid strip of narrow complexes at slightly uneven spacing; the small waves before them vary in shape.

B.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
B.q: A 74-year-old man in cardiac arrest has this rhythm. Which finding on the strip defines it?
opts: Identical wide QRS complexes
Identical wide complexes are monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Here there is no repeating complex to measure.
P waves with no QRS complexes
Upright P waves without QRS complexes are ventricular standstill. There are no P waves on this strip.
A completely flat baseline
A flat line is asystole. This baseline is never still: it is continuous chaotic electrical activity.
No measurable P, QRS or T waves
Correct. In ventricular fibrillation there are no measurable P waves, QRS complexes or T waves, only chaotic irregular activity.
B.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 14
B.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

B.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block Type I, second-degree AV block Type II, third-degree AV block
B.q: A 61-year-old man has second-degree type I block. Which describes his P waves?
opts: Conducted until one is dropped
Correct. In type I the P waves are present, normal and married to the QRS complexes except for the dropped beat.
Absent across the strip
P waves are present in every atrioventricular block; the atria keep firing. Absent P waves point elsewhere.
Unrelated to any QRS complex
P waves unrelated to the QRS complexes are third-degree block. In type I they are conducted until one drops.
Conducted after a constant PR
A constant PR on every conducted beat is type II. In type I the PR lengthens.
B.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 30

B.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, hypocalcemia
B.q: A 63-year-old woman on dialysis missed three sessions. Her 12-lead is shown, with very wide QRS complexes and no visible P waves. Which disturbance best explains it?
opts: Hypokalemia
Hypokalemia flattens T waves and brings out U waves; it does not erase the P waves and widen the QRS like this.
Hypercalcemia
Hypercalcemia shortens the ST segment and QTc; it does not widen the QRS or remove the P waves.
Severe hyperkalemia
Correct. As potassium climbs, the P waves flatten away and the QRS widens toward a sine wave: late, severe hyperkalemia.
Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism gives low-voltage complexes with sinus bradycardia, not this very wide QRS.
B.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 36
B.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

B.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes
B.q: A 59-year-old man's monitor shows this wide-complex rhythm. Which feature marks it as monomorphic?
opts: The rate is above 100 per minute
Both monomorphic and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia run at 100 to 300 per minute, so the rate cannot separate them.
Every complex has the same shape
Correct. Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia is regular, with complexes of one identical shape; the polymorphic form is irregular and changes shape.
The QRS complexes are wide
Every ventricular tachycardia is wide because it starts in the ventricles. Width says ventricular, not which form.
No P waves are visible
P waves are typically absent in both forms. What separates monomorphic from polymorphic is whether the complexes keep one shape.
B.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 5
B.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

B.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
B.q: A 23-year-old man with a known accessory pathway has sudden palpitations. His regular, narrow-complex tachycardia is shown. Which rhythm is this?
opts: Antidromic reentrant tachycardia
Antidromic conduction runs down the accessory pathway first, so the ventricles depolarize abnormally and the tachycardia is wide.
Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia is a wide-complex tachycardia; these complexes are narrow.
Ventricular paced rhythm
A paced rhythm has a spike before each wide QRS and a set rate, not a narrow-complex tachycardia.
Orthodromic reentrant tachycardia
Correct. Orthodromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia conducts down the normal pathway and back up the accessory pathway, producing a regular narrow-complex tachycardia.
B.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 32
B.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

B.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
B.q: A 59-year-old man who had an infarction last year has this complex in lead III. What is the deep first deflection?
opts: A delta wave
A delta wave is a slurred UPSTROKE of the QRS from preexcitation; this is a deep negative deflection before the R wave.
A pathologic Q wave
Correct. The first negative deflection before the R wave is a Q wave; one deeper than 2 mm, or than a quarter of the R wave's height as this one is, is pathologic, a sign of infarction.
An S wave
An S wave is a negative deflection that comes AFTER the R wave. The first negative deflection, before the R, is the Q wave.
An Osborn wave
An Osborn (J) wave is a notch at the END of the QRS, seen in hypothermia and early repolarization, not a deep initial deflection.
B.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 12
B.alt: A single electrocardiogram complex on grid paper

B.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
B.q: A 70-year-old woman with an inferior infarction needs lead V4R. Where is it placed?
opts: Left 5th intercostal space, midclavicular
The left fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line is the standard V4 position; V4R mirrors it on the right.
On the back below the scapula
Electrodes below the scapula are posterior leads (V7 to V9) for a posterior infarction, not V4R.
Right 5th intercostal space, midclavicular
Correct. V4 is moved to the right side of the sternum, fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line, and the tracing is repeated; the right-sided V4 is marked V4R.
Right 2nd intercostal space at the sternum
V4R sits at the fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line, on the right, mirroring the usual V4 position.
B.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 22

B.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
B.q: A 70-year-old man's lead V1 tracing is shown; each QRS is wider than three small boxes. What does this width indicate?
opts: Normal ventricular conduction
Normal ventricular conduction gives a narrow QRS under 0.12 seconds; this complex is wider than that.
A prolonged PR interval
The PR interval is measured before the QRS, from P onset; QRS width reflects ventricular conduction.
A normal Q wave
A Q wave is only the first negative deflection and must be under 0.04 seconds; the whole complex here is too wide.
Abnormal ventricular conduction
Correct. A normal QRS is narrow, under 0.12 seconds (three small boxes); a wider complex means conduction through the ventricles is abnormal.
B.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 31, 61
B.alt: Lead V1 tracing of three beats, each with a broad notched upright complex followed by an inverted wave.

B.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
B.q: A 49-year-old woman's myocardium responds when a stimulus reaches it. Which property is this?
opts: Automaticity
Automaticity is producing an impulse of one's own; responding to an arriving stimulus is excitability.
Conductivity
Conductivity is passing the impulse on from myocyte to myocyte; responding to it is excitability.
Contractility
Contractility is the cell's ability to contract; the electrical response to a stimulus is excitability.
Excitability
Correct. Excitability is the cardiac cell's ability to respond to an impulse or stimulus.
B.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 16

B.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
B.q: A 38-year-old man's tracing shows global concave ST elevation, but also ST depression in leads II and III. How should it be interpreted?
opts: Typical acute pericarditis
Pericarditis has no reciprocal ST depression outside aVR and V1; depression in II and III rules it out as the diagnosis.
Benign early repolarization
Early repolarization also has no reciprocal depression outside aVR and V1, so this depression argues against it too.
Consider an acute infarction instead

Correct. If there is ST depression in any lead other than aVR and V1, or any Q waves in any lead, the tracing cannot be diagnosed as pericarditis and an acute ST-elevation infarction must be considered.
A normal variant in young men
Normal variant ST elevation is early repolarization, which has no reciprocal depression; depression here must raise an infarction.
B.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 5

B.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
B.q: A 78-year-old woman's rate is 40 per minute (normal 60 to 100); her strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Junctional escape rhythm
A junctional escape rhythm is usually narrow at 40 to 60 per minute; these complexes are wide with no P waves.
Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia is a fast run of wide complexes; this wide rhythm is slow and steady, so the Purkinje network is pacing.
Idioventricular rhythm
Correct. A regular, wide-complex rhythm of 20 to 40 per minute with no P waves is idioventricular rhythm: the Purkinje network is pacing.
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia has upright P waves married to each QRS; here there are no P waves and the complexes are wide.
B.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 75, 76, 77, 78
B.alt: Pink grid strip with four widely spaced broad complexes, each followed by a wave in the opposite direction, and no waves between them.

B.io: Compare and contrast ECG manifestations of electrolyte abnormalities.
B.q: A 60-year-old man with a high serum calcium has the 12-lead shown. Which phase of the cardiac action potential is shortened to produce it?
opts: Phase 0
Phase 0 is the rapid sodium upstroke; calcium disorders act on the phase 2 plateau.
Phase 3
Phase 3 is the repolarization slowed by amiodarone's potassium-channel block, which prolongs the QT; calcium acts on phase 2.
Phase 2
Correct. Hypercalcemia shortens phase 2 (the plateau), which shortens the ST segment and the QTc; hypocalcemia prolongs the same phase.
Phase 4
Phase 4 is the resting phase between beats; the ST segment reflects phase 2.
B.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 42; tracing from Slide 43
B.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

B.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
B.q: A 63-year-old woman has ST elevation limited to V1 and V2. Which region of the heart do these leads view?
opts: Anterior wall
The anterior wall is viewed by V3 and V4. V1 and V2 view the septum.
Lateral wall
The lateral wall is viewed by I, aVL, V5 and V6, not by V1 and V2, which are the septal leads.
Inferior wall
The inferior wall is viewed by II, III and aVF; elevation limited to V1 and V2 is septal.
Septal wall
Correct. V1 and V2 are the septal leads; elevation limited to them localizes to the septal wall, which has no reciprocal leads on the standard 12-lead.
B.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 15

B.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: left ventricular hypertrophy, right ventricular hypertrophy
B.q: A 45-year-old woman with pulmonary hypertension has this electrocardiogram. Which finding does it show?
opts: Right ventricular hypertrophy
Correct. More R wave than S wave in V1 and V2, a strain pattern there, right axis deviation and right atrial enlargement: right ventricular hypertrophy.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy gives deep S waves in V1 and V2 with tall lateral R waves. V1 here is dominantly positive.
Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block is an exclusion for this diagnosis and needs a QRS of 0.12 seconds or longer with an rSR in V1; here the tall R comes with strain and right axis deviation.
Left atrial enlargement
Left atrial enlargement is a P wave finding (P mitrale). The striking change here is in the QRS of V1 and V2.
B.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 34
B.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

B.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
B.q: A 55-year-old woman has chest pain and the fast rhythm strip shown, with no visible TP segment. To judge ST elevation, what should the J point be compared with?
opts: The TP segment
The TP segment is the usual baseline, but at this rate it has disappeared, which is exactly when the onset of the QRS is used instead.
The peak of the T wave
The peak of the T wave is not a baseline at all; ST deviation is measured against the resting baseline.
The top of the R wave
The R-wave peak measures QRS amplitude, not ST deviation. A baseline is needed, and here that is the start of the QRS.
The onset of the QRS

Correct. The J point is normally compared to the TP segment, but at fast rates the TP segment can be hard to find, and it is then appropriate to compare the J point to the beginning of the QRS complex.
B.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 6
B.alt: A single-lead rhythm strip on grid paper at a fast rate

B.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
B.q: A 67-year-old man's QRS is 0.12 seconds or longer (normal under 0.12). His V1 and V6 complexes are shown. Which block is this?
opts: Right bundle branch block
Correct. V1 is an rSR pattern whose first deflection back from the J point is positive, and V6 has a slurred S wave: right bundle branch block.
Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block makes V1 an rS pattern ending negative, with a notched R in V6.
Left posterior fascicular block
A fascicular block keeps the QRS narrow. This QRS is 0.12 seconds or longer.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy gives deep S waves in V1 and tall lateral R waves at a normal duration.
B.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 16
B.alt: Two drawn complexes, leads V1 and V6

B.io: Compare and contrast sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
B.q: A 79-year-old woman's strip is shown; her sinus node stops and restarts. What separates sinus arrest from sinus pause?
opts: At least three missed cycles
Correct. Both reset the node and neither marches out; sinus arrest is the one in which at least three cardiac cycles have been missed.
P to P intervals march out
Neither pause nor arrest marches out, because the node resets; marching out is sinus exit block.
A blocked sinus impulse
A blocked impulse is sinus exit block; pause and arrest are the node stopping, separated by the number of missed cycles.
A wide QRS after the gap
The returning beats are sinus beats with narrow QRS; the difference is three or more missed cycles.
B.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 95
B.alt: Rhythm strip with four narrow complexes, a long flat baseline several cycles wide, then four more complexes.

B.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: left ventricular hypertrophy, right ventricular hypertrophy
B.q: A 70-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram. Her S wave in V2 is 30 millimeters and her R wave in V5 is 19 millimeters (normal sum under 35). Which finding does it show?
opts: Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy shows more R than S wave in V1 and V2. These are deep S waves with tall lateral R waves.
Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block is a wide-QRS rSR pattern in V1. The finding here is voltage.
Left atrial enlargement
Left atrial enlargement is a P wave finding. The criterion met here is a QRS voltage sum.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Correct. The deeper S wave in V1 or V2 added to the taller R wave in V5 or V6 is 49 millimeters, at least 35: left ventricular hypertrophy.
B.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 38
B.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

B.io: Correlate ECG findings with clinical implications of ventricular arrhythmias and AV blocks
B.q: A 59-year-old man collapses. No carotid pulse is felt, and the monitor shows this. What is the rhythm?
opts: Normal sinus rhythm
The tracing looks like sinus rhythm, but a rhythm with no pulse is not sinus rhythm. Organized activity without a pulse is pulseless electrical activity.
Ventricular standstill
Ventricular standstill shows P waves with no QRS complexes. Every P wave here is followed by a QRS and a T wave.
Asystole
Asystole has no electrical activity. This monitor shows organized P waves, QRS complexes and T waves.
Pulseless electrical activity
Correct. Organized electrical activity on the monitor with no mechanical activity, no pulse, is pulseless electrical activity, whatever rhythm it looks like.
B.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 16
B.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

B.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
B.q: A 52-year-old man's monitor prints this six-second strip. What is his ventricular rate?
opts: 80 per minute
Eighty would be eight complexes in six seconds; this strip carries nine, so the rate is 90.
90 per minute
Correct. Nine QRS complexes fall between the three-second markers, and nine times ten is 90 per minute (the six-second method).
100 per minute
One hundred would need ten complexes in six seconds; there are nine here, giving 90.
60 per minute
Sixty would be six complexes; nine QRS complexes in six seconds times ten is 90 per minute.
B.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 44, 45
B.alt: Six-second rhythm strip with three-second tick marks along the top and regularly spaced narrow complexes.

B.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
B.q: A 69-year-old woman's limb leads are shown, with Q waves and ST elevation in III and aVF. Which artery most likely supplies the affected wall?
opts: Left anterior descending
The left anterior descending artery supplies the front of the left ventricle and the front of the septum, which the V leads (V1 to V4) view.
Left circumflex artery
The circumflex supplies the side and back of the left ventricle; its occlusion shows in the lateral leads or as a posterior infarction.
Right coronary artery
Correct. III and aVF view the inferior wall, and the right coronary artery supplies the bottom (inferior) portion of the left ventricle along with the right atrium and right ventricle.
Left main coronary artery
The left main divides into the circumflex and the left anterior descending; it does not supply the inferior wall that III and aVF view.
B.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 4; tracing from Slide 13
B.alt: Limb-lead electrocardiogram (leads I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF) on grid paper

B.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: myocardial ischemia, myocardial injury, myocardial infarction
B.q: A 49-year-old woman has chest pain and the 12-lead shown. Besides ST elevation, which early ischemic finding is visible in V1 to V4?
opts: Hyperacute T waves
Correct. The T waves are broad, increased in amplitude and symmetrical, large enough to hold the QRS inside them: hyperacute T waves alongside the ST elevation.
Pathologic Q waves
Pathologic Q waves mark tissue death and are deep and wide initial negative deflections; the striking change in these leads is the size of the T waves.
Inverted T waves
These T waves point upward and are enlarged. T-wave inversion is a different, later sign of ischemia.
Prominent U waves
Prominent U waves are a hypokalemia finding that follows the T wave; here the T wave itself is broad, tall and symmetrical.
B.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 11
B.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

B.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: digoxin toxicity, amiodarone toxicity, tricyclic antidepressant toxicity
B.q: An 84-year-old man on digoxin has the rhythm strip shown. Which abnormality is the most common one in digoxin toxicity?
opts: A delta wave with a short PR
A delta wave with a short PR is Wolff-Parkinson-White preexcitation, not digoxin toxicity.
Frequent premature ventricular beats
Correct. Digoxin toxicity inhibits the sodium-potassium pump and makes cells abnormally excitable; frequent premature ventricular complexes are its most common abnormality.
Coved ST elevation in V1 to V3
Coved V1 to V3 elevation is type 1 Brugada, an inherited sodium-channel disease.
Osborn waves
Osborn waves are terminal QRS notches of hypothermia and early repolarization.
B.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 47
B.alt: A single-lead rhythm strip on grid paper

B.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
B.q: A 62-year-old woman had V4, V5 and V6 moved to her back and the tracing repeated, as shown. What is this recording often called?
opts: A 15-lead electrocardiogram
Correct. Moving V4 to V6 to the back as V7, V8 and V9 and repeating the tracing gives what is at times called a 15-lead electrocardiogram, the posterior tracing.
A right-sided electrocardiogram
A right-sided tracing moves V4 to the right fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line (V4R) to look at the right ventricle, not to the back.
A 3-lead rhythm strip
