A rhythm strip monitors rate and rhythm in a few leads. The posterior tracing is a full 12-lead with three chest electrodes relocated.
A reversed limb-lead tracing
No limb electrode is moved here; the three lateral chest electrodes are relocated to the back to view the posterior wall.
B.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 19; tracing from Slide 21
B.alt: Electrocardiogram with three chest-lead labels crossed out and handwritten replacements (V7, V8, V9)

B.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
B.q: A 25-year-old woman has a preexcitation syndrome. Which is the most common one?
opts: Brugada syndrome
Brugada syndrome is an inherited sodium-channel disease of the right ventricular outflow tract, not a preexcitation syndrome.
Early repolarization
Benign early repolarization is a normal variant ST elevation, not an accessory pathway syndrome.
Left bundle branch block
A left bundle branch block is delayed, not early, ventricular activation.
Wolff-Parkinson-White
Correct. The most common preexcitation syndrome is Wolff-Parkinson-White, in which the accessory pathway is the bundle of Kent.
B.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 25

B.io: Recognize sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia
B.q: A 31-year-old man's regular strip is shown; R waves sit two large boxes apart. What is the rate (normal 60 to 100 per minute)?
opts: 100 per minute
One hundred would be three large boxes apart; two large boxes gives 150.
300 per minute
Three hundred would be an R wave on every large box; two boxes apart halves that to 150.
150 per minute
Correct. By the 300 method, 300 divided by two large boxes is 150 per minute; with sinus P waves that is sinus tachycardia.
75 per minute
Seventy-five would be four large boxes apart; two large boxes gives 150 per minute.
B.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 52, 80
B.alt: Rhythm strip with closely and evenly spaced narrow complexes, each with a small wave before it.

B.io: Recognize normal sinus rhythm
B.q: A 34-year-old woman's routine strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus arrhythmia has the same P waves but irregular R to R intervals; this strip is regular.
Normal sinus rhythm
Correct. The rhythm is regular, at about 75 to 80 per minute, with normal P waves married to narrow QRS complexes and a normal, constant PR.
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia is below 60 per minute; this strip's rate is about 75 to 80.
Sinus exit block
Sinus exit block drops whole cycles, leaving gaps; this strip has no missing beats.
B.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 72, 73
B.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip with evenly spaced narrow complexes, each preceded by a small rounded upright wave.

B.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, SVT, atrial tachycardia
B.q: A 75-year-old man's strip is shown; the flutter waves are constant but the R to R intervals vary. How should it be documented?
opts: Flutter with 2:1 conduction
A fixed 2:1 ratio would give evenly spaced QRS complexes; here the spacing changes, so the conduction is variable.
Atrial fibrillation
Fibrillation has no organized waves; this baseline keeps its regular flutter waves, only the conduction varies.
Flutter with 4:1 conduction
A fixed ratio of any number gives a regular rhythm; unequal R to R intervals mean variable conduction.
Flutter with variable conduction
Correct. When the ratio of flutter waves to QRS complexes keeps changing, the rhythm is irregular and is documented as atrial flutter with variable conduction.
B.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 25, 30, 31
B.alt: Gray grid strip of four narrow complexes at unequal spacing, with a continuous rounded zigzag baseline between them.

B.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
B.q: A 52-year-old man's strip is shown; the arrows mark two beats. What are the marked beats?
opts: Premature ventricular complexes
A premature ventricular complex would be wide with no P wave; the marked beats are narrow.
Premature atrial complexes
Correct. Each marked beat comes early with a narrow QRS and a P wave of different shape: a premature atrial complex, from an atrial site outside the sinus node.
Junctional escape beats
An escape beat arrives late, after a pause; the marked beats come early.
Sinus exit block
Sinus exit block leaves a gap with no beat at all; here extra beats arrive early.
B.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 6, 7
B.alt: Rhythm strip of regularly spaced narrow complexes; two downward arrows mark beats that arrive sooner than expected.

B.io: Discuss related anatomy and physiology of ventricular conduction abnormalities and chamber enlargement
B.q: A 64-year-old man has a new wide-complex tachycardia with extreme axis deviation. Which rhythm does that axis raise suspicion for?
opts: Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia uses the normal pathway and leaves the axis normal. Extreme deviation suggests a ventricular origin.
Left anterior fascicular block
Left anterior fascicular block causes left axis deviation with a narrow QRS, not a wide tachycardia in no man's land.
Ventricular tachycardia
Correct. A ventricular arrhythmia is one of the causes of extreme axis deviation; a wide-complex tachycardia in no man's land points toward ventricular tachycardia.
Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement changes the P wave, not the QRS axis of a tachycardia.
B.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 21

B.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block Type I, second-degree AV block Type II, third-degree AV block
B.q: A 41-year-old man has this strip, and his rhythm looks like sinus at first glance. Which single measurement makes the diagnosis?
opts: The QRS duration
The QRS can be narrow or wide in first-degree block, so it does not make the diagnosis. The PR interval does.
The P-P interval
The P waves are regular, as in any sinus rhythm. That says nothing about conduction through the atrioventricular node.
The PR interval
Correct. This is first-degree block, and the PR interval is all that diagnoses it: a sinus rhythm with a PR beyond 0.2 seconds.
The heart rate
The rate is slow or normal in first-degree block, so rate cannot make the diagnosis. The PR interval does.
B.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 28
B.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

B.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
B.q: A 74-year-old woman with a pacemaker has this strip. Which pacing does it show?
opts: Ventricular pacing
Ventricular pacing puts the spike right before a wide QRS with an opposite-direction T wave. These QRS complexes are narrow and normal.
Atrial and ventricular pacing
Dual pacing shows two spikes per beat, one before the P wave and one before the QRS. This strip shows one spike per beat.
Atrial pacing
Correct. A pacer spike followed by a normal P-QRS-T cycle is an atrial paced rhythm: the pacemaker takes over for the sinoatrial node.
No pacing, sinus rhythm
Each cycle here starts with a pacer spike, so the pacemaker, not the sinoatrial node, is firing.
B.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 19
B.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

B.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular escape rhythms
B.q: An 80-year-old woman has a junctional escape beat on her strip. When does such a beat occur?
opts: When the sinus node fails or slows
Correct. Junctional escape beats occur when the sinoatrial node fails to fire or fires too slowly, so the junction steps in.
When junctional automaticity rises
Increased junctional automaticity produces early beats, premature junctional complexes; escape beats follow sinus failure.
When the ventricles fire early
Early ventricular firing is a premature ventricular complex; a junctional escape beat answers a failing sinus node.
When an atrial circuit reenters
Atrial reentry causes flutter; escape beats appear when the sinus node fails or slows.
B.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 52

B.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
B.q: A 77-year-old man is pulseless. His monitor shows this. What is the rhythm?
opts: Ventricular standstill
Correct. Obvious upright P waves march across the strip with no QRS complexes: the atria contract but the ventricles do not, with no pulse.
Asystole
Asystole is a flat line with no electrical activity. This strip has regular P waves, so the atria are still firing.
Third-degree atrioventricular block
Third-degree block keeps a slow escape QRS beating independently of the P waves. Here there are no QRS complexes at all.
Pulseless electrical activity
Pulseless electrical activity is an organized rhythm with QRS complexes but no pulse. This strip has no QRS complexes.
B.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 17
B.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

B.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
B.q: A 46-year-old woman's strip is shown; the arrow points to a deflection after one QRS. What is that early beat?
opts: A premature atrial complex
A premature atrial complex has an early upright P wave before its QRS; here the P falls after it.
A premature ventricular complex
A premature ventricular complex is wide with an opposite-direction T wave; this early beat is narrow.
A premature junctional complex
Correct. The early narrow beat has its P wave after the QRS (a retrograde P wave), which places its origin in the atrioventricular junction.
A ventricular escape complex
A ventricular escape complex is wide and late; this beat is narrow and early.
B.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 50, 51
B.alt: Green grid strip of narrow complexes; an arrow below one early beat points to a small notch just after its complex.

B.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement
B.q: A 66-year-old man's V1 shows a biphasic P wave with a small positive first part and a large negative second part. What does it indicate?
opts: Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement is the reverse in V1: the positive first part is the larger one.
Left atrial enlargement
Correct. A biphasic P wave in V1 with a small positive initial deflection and a large negative terminal deflection is left atrial enlargement.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS finding, more R wave than S wave in V1 and V2.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS voltage finding, not a biphasic P wave in V1.
B.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 30

B.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of AV nodal and infranodal conduction abnormalities
B.q: A 77-year-old woman has complete heart block. Which two pacemakers drive her heart?
opts: The sinoatrial node and an escape
Correct. There are two independent pacemakers: the sinoatrial node for the atria, and either the atrioventricular junction or the Purkinje and bundle-branch fibers for the ventricles.
Two foci within the ventricles
Only the ventricular pacemaker is below the block. The atria are still driven by the sinoatrial node.
Two foci within the atria
The atria are driven by the sinoatrial node alone. The ventricles need their own escape pacemaker below the block.
The sinoatrial node alone
The sinoatrial node cannot reach the ventricles through a complete block, so a second pacemaker must take over below it.
B.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 42

B.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
B.q: A 71-year-old man has this electrocardiogram. Which conduction abnormality does it show?
opts: Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block shows a positive deflection before the J point in V1 (rSR) and slurred lateral S waves. V1 here is negative.
Left anterior fascicular block
Left anterior fascicular block has a narrow QRS with left axis deviation. These complexes are wide.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Hypertrophy raises voltage with a normal QRS duration. These complexes are wide, with lateral notching.
Left bundle branch block
Correct. A wide QRS, a negative first deflection back from the J point in V1, notched lateral QRS complexes and no lateral Q waves: left bundle branch block.
B.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 13
B.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

B.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
B.q: A 30-year-old man of Southeast Asian descent fainted at rest. His 12-lead is shown. Which diagnosis fits the pattern in V1 and V2?
opts: Type 2 Brugada pattern
Type 2 is the saddleback shape, with the ST segment dipping before the T wave; these right precordial leads are coved.
Type 1 Brugada pattern
Correct. Coved (convex) ST elevation isolated to V1 to V3 in a young man of Southeast Asian descent is the type 1, coved-shaped Brugada pattern.
Anteroseptal infarction
An anteroseptal infarction elevates V1 to V4 in a patient with ischemic symptoms; the coved shape confined to V1 to V3 in a young man is Brugada.
Benign early repolarization
Early repolarization is global and concave with J-point notching, not coved elevation confined to the right precordial leads.

B.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of sinus node dysfunction
B.q: A 7-year-old boy's heart rate rises each time he inhales. What causes the rise?
opts: A rise in vagal tone
More vagal tone would slow the heart, as happens on exhalation; inspiration suppresses vagal tone.
Blocked sinus impulses
Blocked impulses drop whole cycles (sinus exit block); sinus arrhythmia is rate variation from vagal tone.
Suppression of vagal tone
Correct. Inspiration lowers intrathoracic and arterial pressure, the baroreceptors respond, vagal tone is suppressed and the heart rate increases.
Higher intrathoracic pressure
Intrathoracic pressure falls on inspiration, not rises; that drop leads to suppressed vagal tone.

B.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
B.q: A 62-year-old woman's rate is 70 per minute (normal 60 to 100); her strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Junctional escape rhythm
The escape rhythm runs 40 to 60 per minute; this junctional rhythm at 70 is accelerated.
Accelerated junctional rhythm
Correct. Inverted P waves married to narrow QRS complexes with a short PR at 70 per minute make an accelerated junctional rhythm (60 to 100).
Accelerated idioventricular rhythm
Accelerated idioventricular rhythm is wide with no P waves; these complexes are narrow.
Normal sinus rhythm
A sinus rhythm at 70 would have upright P waves and a normal PR, not inverted P waves with a short PR.

B.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
B.q: A 64-year-old woman's limb leads are being read for a posterior fascicular block. Which lead has no significance in identifying it?
opts: Lead I
Lead I matters: it is mostly negative in left posterior fascicular block, with an r wave.
Lead II
Correct. Lead II has no significance in identifying left posterior fascicular block; it is usually positive or biphasic.
Lead III
Lead III matters: it is mostly positive, with a q wave, in left posterior fascicular block.
Lead aVF
aVF matters: it is mostly positive, which with a negative lead I gives right axis deviation.

B.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
B.q: A 58-year-old woman with lung disease has this electrocardiogram. What is her electrical axis?
opts: Normal axis
A normal axis has a mostly positive QRS in both lead I and aVF; the normal range is -30 to +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Left axis deviation
Left axis deviation has lead I mostly positive and aVF mostly negative, an axis beyond -30 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Right axis deviation
Correct. Lead I is mostly negative and aVF is mostly positive: right axis deviation.
Extreme axis deviation
Extreme axis deviation, no man's land, has both lead I and aVF mostly negative. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.

B.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block, third-degree AV block
B.q: A 73-year-old man's regular P waves appear to march through his QRS-T complexes. Which block does this describe?
opts: Second-degree type II (Mobitz II)
Type II conducts most P waves with a fixed PR. The P waves are tied to the QRS complexes except for the dropped beats.
Third-degree block
Correct. Regular P-P intervals unrelated to regular R-R intervals, with P waves that march through the QRS-T complexes, are the hallmark of third-degree block.
First-degree block
First-degree block keeps every P wave married to a QRS, after a long PR.
Second-degree type I
Type I P waves are married to the QRS complexes, with a lengthening PR, until one drops.

B.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: COPD/COLD, pulmonary embolism, hypothermia
B.q: A 75-year-old man was found outdoors on a winter night. His 12-lead is shown. What are the notches at the end of each QRS?
opts: Osborn waves
Correct. Below 32°C (90°F), Osborn (J) waves appear as notches at the end of the QRS, and they are frequently mistaken for an ST-elevation infarction.
Delta waves
Delta waves are slurred upstrokes at the start of the QRS in preexcitation; these notches sit at its end.
Prominent U waves
U waves follow the T wave and are a hypokalemia sign; these notches are at the junction of the QRS and ST segment.
Pacing artifacts
Pacing artifacts are sharp spikes BEFORE a paced QRS, not rounded notches after it.

B.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
B.q: A 49-year-old woman collapses on the ward, and this rhythm is on her monitor. What is it?
opts: Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia is regular, with complexes of one shape. These complexes change shape and amplitude from beat to beat.
Ventricular fibrillation
Ventricular fibrillation is chaotic, with no measurable QRS. This strip still has large ventricular complexes, twisting in a pattern.
Torsades de pointes
Correct. An irregular, polymorphic ventricular tachycardia whose complexes swell and shrink as they twist around the baseline is torsades de pointes.
Ventricular standstill
Ventricular standstill shows P waves marching across with no QRS at all. This strip is full of rapid ventricular complexes.

B.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

B.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: Benign Early Repolarization (BER), acute pericarditis, long QT syndrome
B.q: A 34-year-old man has had chest pain for two days. His 12-lead is shown. Which diagnosis best fits the tracing?
opts: Acute pericarditis
Correct. Global concave ST elevation with PR-segment depression, PR elevation in aVR and no reciprocal ST depression outside aVR and V1 is acute pericarditis.
Inferior ST-elevation infarction
An inferior infarction elevates II, III and aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL; this elevation is global and concave with no reciprocal changes.
Benign early repolarization
Early repolarization also shows global concave elevation, but not the PR-segment depression seen here; it carries J-point notching instead.
Brugada syndrome
Brugada changes are isolated to V1 to V3 (coved or saddleback elevation); this tracing's elevation is global.

B.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
B.q: A 36-year-old man is studied for a reentry rhythm. In most people, which internodal tract truly attaches to the atrioventricular node?
opts: The middle tract
The middle tract usually terminates somewhere within the right atrium; it is the fast, superior anterior tract that attaches.
The inferior posterior tract
The inferior posterior (slow) tract usually ends within the right atrium; in most people only the fast tract attaches.
All three, equally
There are three internodal pathways, but in most people only the superior anterior (fast) tract reaches the atrioventricular node.
The superior anterior tract
Correct. In most people only the superior anterior tract, the fast tract, truly attaches to the atrioventricular node; the other two end in the right atrium.
B.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 9

B.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
B.q: A 57-year-old woman with chest pain has ST elevation in II, III and aVF but no reciprocal depression anywhere. How should the missing reciprocal changes be read?
opts: They rule out an infarction
Absence of reciprocal changes is not a rule-out criterion. ST elevation of 1 mm in two contiguous leads defines the infarction with or without them.
They do not exclude ischemia
Correct. Reciprocal changes confirm ischemia when ST elevation is present, but their absence does not exclude cardiac ischemia; an ST-elevation infarction is considered with or without them.
They prove lead misplacement
Missing reciprocal changes are common and do not imply a technical error; the elevation still has to be taken seriously.
They confirm benign repolarization
Localized ST elevation in II, III and aVF in a patient with chest pain is not benign; the lack of reciprocal changes does not change that.

B.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement: left atrial enlargement, right atrial enlargement
B.q: A 66-year-old man with emphysema has these limb leads. Which chamber finding do they show?
opts: Left atrial enlargement
Left atrial enlargement makes the limb-lead P wave wide and humped, at least 0.12 seconds, not tall and peaked.
Right atrial enlargement
Correct. Tall, peaked, upright P waves in the limb leads, taller than 2.5 millimeters, are P pulmonale: right atrial enlargement.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is read from V1 and V2 (more R wave than S wave). These limb leads show a P wave change.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS voltage finding. The striking change here is in the P waves.

B.io: Review ECG lead placement
B.q: A 56-year-old man's inferior wall is in question. Which leads look at the inferior wall?
opts: II, III and augmented vector foot
Correct. Leads II, III and aVF (augmented vector foot) look at the inferior wall.
V1 and V2
V1 and V2 look at the septal wall; the inferior leads are II, III and aVF.
V3 and V4
V3 and V4 look at the anterior wall of the left ventricle; the inferior leads are II, III and aVF.
I, augmented vector left, V5, V6
Leads I, aVL (augmented vector left), V5 and V6 look at the lateral wall; the inferior wall is II, III and aVF.
B.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 69, 70

B.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
B.q: A 58-year-old man has ST elevation in V3 and V4 only. Which region of the heart do these leads view?
opts: Septal wall
The septal leads are V1 and V2. V3 and V4 face the anterior wall.
Lateral wall
The lateral leads are I, aVL, V5 and V6; V3 and V4 sit in front of the anterior wall instead.
Posterior wall
No standard lead faces the posterior wall; it is seen through reciprocal depression in V1 to V4 and confirmed with V7 to V9.
Anterior wall
Correct. V3 and V4 are the anterior leads; together with V1 and V2 they make the anteroseptal territory V1 to V4.

B.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of supraventricular arrhythmias
B.q: A 30-year-old man has typical atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia. How does the circuit travel?
opts: Down the fast tract, up the slow
Down the fast and up the slow is the atypical form, in which retrograde P waves are clearly visible.
Around the right atrium
A circuit around the right atrium is atrial flutter, which produces a sawtooth baseline.
Through Bachmann's bundle
Bachmann's bundle carries impulses between the atria; the reentry circuit uses the slow and fast tracts.
Down the slow tract, up the fast
Correct. In the typical form the circuit travels counterclockwise down the slow tract and up the fast tract; P waves are absent or buried at the end of the QRS.
B.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 39

B.io: Recognize common supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation
B.q: A 78-year-old man's strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Atrial flutter
Flutter shows an organized sawtooth baseline; this baseline is chaotic and the spacing unpredictable.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular too, but has distinct P waves of three shapes; here there are none.
Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus arrhythmia keeps a normal P wave before every QRS; here no P waves can be found.
Atrial fibrillation
Correct. Narrow complexes at irregularly irregular intervals over a disorganized baseline with no P waves (fibrillatory waves only) is atrial fibrillation.
B.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 32, 33, 34, 35
B.alt: Pink grid strip of narrow complexes at unpredictable spacing, with a wavy, shapeless baseline and no distinct waves before them.

B.io: Define: normal axis, left axis deviation, right axis deviation
B.q: A 59-year-old woman's axis lies beyond -30 degrees (normal -30 to +90). Which category is this?
opts: Left axis deviation
Correct. Beyond -30 degrees, toward -90, is left axis deviation; the normal range ends at -30 degrees.
Normal axis
The normal axis stops at -30 degrees. An axis beyond -30 has deviated to the left.
Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation lies beyond +90 degrees, on the opposite side of the circle.
Extreme axis deviation
Extreme axis deviation lies between -90 and 180 degrees, where both lead I and aVF are negative.

B.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
B.q: A 53-year-old woman's strip is read at standard speed. How long is one large box?
opts: 0.2 seconds
Correct. A large box is five small boxes, 5 millimeters tall and 0.2 seconds wide.
0.04 seconds
That is a single small box; five of them make one large box of 0.2 seconds.
0.5 seconds
That is two and a half large boxes; each large box is 0.2 seconds.
1 second
One second takes five large boxes; each large box is 0.2 seconds.

C.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of supraventricular arrhythmias
C.q: A 76-year-old man develops atrial fibrillation. What is happening in his atria?
opts: Many sites fire chaotically
Correct. Atrial fibrillation is irregular electrical activity of multiple sites within the atria, which suppresses the sinoatrial node.
One reentry loop circulates
A single reentry circuit, usually in the right atrium, is atrial flutter; fibrillation is many sites firing chaotically.
Three foci take turns
Three competing foci with distinct P waves is a wandering pacemaker or multifocal atrial tachycardia.
The sinus node fires faster
In fibrillation the sinus node is suppressed, not speeded up; chaotic atrial sites take over.
C.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 32

C.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
C.q: A 62-year-old woman has chest pain. Her 12-lead is shown, with ST depression in V1 to V3 and no ST elevation anywhere. Which is the next best step?
opts: Record posterior leads V7 to V9
Correct. Isolated ST depression in V1 to V4 with no elevation anywhere is a reciprocal change for a posterior infarction until proven otherwise, so a posterior (15-lead) tracing is obtained.
Record right-sided lead V4R
V4R checks for right ventricular involvement in an inferior infarction. The pattern here (isolated anterior depression) calls for the posterior leads.
Repeat the standard 12 leads only
The standard leads have no camera on the back of the heart; repeating them cannot show the posterior wall that this depression may be mirroring.
Treat as anterior ischemia only
Isolated V1 to V4 depression must be presumed reciprocal to a posterior infarction until proven otherwise; settling for anterior ischemia risks missing it.

C.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, hypocalcemia
C.q: A 45-year-old woman's leads V4 to V6 are shown. What are the arrowed waves that follow each T wave?
opts: Delta waves
A delta wave slurs the start of the QRS in preexcitation; these waves come after the T wave.
U waves
Correct. A small wave after the T wave is a U wave. Prominent U waves, with T-wave flattening, are classic signs of hypokalemia, which prolongs repolarization.
Osborn waves
Osborn waves are notches at the end of the QRS in hypothermia, not waves after the T wave.
Second P waves
These waves follow the T wave closely in every beat; prominent waves in that position are U waves.

C.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: left ventricular hypertrophy, right ventricular hypertrophy
C.q: A 54-year-old woman has this V1 complex. What does its ST segment and T wave show?
opts: A strain pattern
Correct. A strain pattern is the shape of the ST segment from the J point into an inverted, asymmetrical T wave, seen in V1 and V2.
Peaked P waves
Peaked P waves are right atrial enlargement, a P wave finding. The finding here is after the QRS.
Lateral notching
Notching is a QRS finding of left bundle branch block in the lateral leads. This is the ST and T wave in V1.
A normal T wave
A normal T wave is upright and symmetric. This one is inverted and asymmetric after a sloping ST segment.

C.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
C.q: A 58-year-old woman's six-second strip is shown. How is her atrial rate found from it?
opts: Count QRS complexes, multiply by ten
That gives the ventricular rate; the atrial rate uses the P waves counted in six seconds.
Divide 300 by the P waves
The 300 method divides 300 by large boxes between waves, not by a count; the atrial rate is P waves times ten.
Count T waves, multiply by ten
T waves are ventricular repolarization; the atrial rate comes from the P waves in six seconds.
Count P waves, multiply by ten
Correct. In the six-second method, P waves counted in six seconds times ten give the atrial rate; QRS complexes times ten give the ventricular rate.

C.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
C.q: An 83-year-old man's rate is 40 per minute (normal 60 to 100); his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Junctional escape rhythm
Junctional escape rhythms are typically narrow, from the atrioventricular node; these complexes are wide.
Idioventricular rhythm
Correct. Regular, wide complexes with opposite-direction T waves, no P waves and a rate of 20 to 40 per minute make idioventricular rhythm.
Sinus arrest
Sinus arrest is a long flat gap in a sinus rhythm; this is a steady, slow, wide rhythm.
Premature ventricular complexes
Premature ventricular complexes interrupt an underlying rhythm early; here every beat is wide and evenly spaced.

C.io: Define: normal axis, left axis deviation, right axis deviation
C.q: A 48-year-old woman's lead I QRS is mostly negative and her aVF QRS is mostly positive. Which axis is this?
opts: Normal axis
A normal axis has a mostly positive QRS in both lead I and aVF; the normal range is -30 to +90 degrees. Here lead I is negative.
Right axis deviation
Correct. Lead I mostly negative with aVF mostly positive is right axis deviation.
Left axis deviation
Left axis deviation has lead I mostly positive and aVF mostly negative, an axis beyond -30 degrees. Here the pattern is reversed.
Extreme axis deviation
Extreme axis deviation, no man's land, has both lead I and aVF mostly negative. Here aVF is positive.

C.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block, third-degree AV block
C.q: An 82-year-old woman has this strip. Which relationship between the P waves and the QRS complexes does it show?
opts: A QRS after each P at a long PR
One QRS per P wave at a long PR is first-degree block. Here the P waves outnumber the QRS complexes.
A PR that lengthens until one drops
Progressive lengthening to a dropped beat is second-degree type I. Here the PR is never consistent.
None: each beats at its own regular rate
Correct. In third-degree block regular P-P intervals are unrelated to regular R-R intervals; atrial and ventricular activity are totally independent.
A constant PR with occasional drops
A constant PR with dropped beats is second-degree type II. Here no PR interval repeats.

C.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

C.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
C.q: A 30-year-old man with a known accessory pathway has a regular, wide, monomorphic tachycardia, shown here. Which rhythm is most likely?
opts: Antidromic reentrant tachycardia
Correct. Antidromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia conducts down the accessory pathway and back up the normal pathway, producing a regular, monomorphic, wide tachycardia.
Orthodromic reentrant tachycardia
Orthodromic reentry goes down the normal pathway, so its tachycardia is narrow.
Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia has normal P waves before narrow QRS complexes; this is a wide-complex tachycardia.
Ventricular paced rhythm
A paced rhythm shows a spike before each QRS at a programmed rate, not a wide tachycardia like this.

C.io: Discuss related anatomy and physiology of ventricular conduction abnormalities and chamber enlargement
C.q: A 75-year-old woman has left bundle branch block. Which ventricle depolarizes first?
opts: The left ventricle
The left bundle is the blocked one, so the left ventricle depolarizes late, after the impulse crosses from the right.
The right ventricle
Correct. Impulses travel down the right bundle normally, so the right ventricle contracts first; the left must wait for myocyte-to-myocyte spread.
Both at the same time
Simultaneous depolarization is normal conduction. In a bundle branch block the ventricles contract in sequence.
The septum, left to right
Normal septal depolarization runs left to right, but in left bundle branch block the septal fascicle is blocked too.

C.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of sinus node dysfunction
C.q: A 67-year-old woman's strip shows a sinus pause. Why do the P to P intervals fail to march out after the gap?
opts: The impulse is blocked
A blocked impulse is sinus exit block, where the node keeps time and beats do march out.
The sinoatrial node resets
Correct. During a sinus pause the node stops firing and starts back up, so the cardiac cycle is reset and the P to P intervals no longer march out.
An atrial focus takes over
The beats after the pause still have the same sinus P waves; the sinus node has simply reset.
The atrioventricular node fails
Atrioventricular failure would leave P waves without QRS complexes; in a pause the sinus node itself stops and resets.

C.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
C.q: A 76-year-old woman in cardiac arrest is monitored, and this strip is recorded. What change does it show?
opts: Ventricular tachycardia becoming sinus rhythm
Sinus rhythm would show organized P, QRS and T waves. The right side of this strip is a flat line with no activity.
Asystole becoming ventricular fibrillation
The order is reversed: the strip starts with chaotic waves and ends flat. That is fibrillation becoming asystole.
Torsades becoming ventricular tachycardia
Both of those have large wide complexes. Here small chaotic waves end in a flat line with no complexes at all.
Ventricular fibrillation becoming asystole
Correct. Chaotic fibrillatory waves on the left give way to a flat line on the right: ventricular fibrillation degenerating into asystole.

C.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, SVT, atrial tachycardia
C.q: A 33-year-old man's regular narrow tachycardia is shown; the highlighted notch ends each QRS. What is the notch?
opts: A true S wave
A true S wave is part of ventricular depolarization; this notch is a retrograde P wave buried at the end of the QRS.
A flutter wave
Flutter waves form a continuous sawtooth between complexes; here a single notch ends each QRS.
A buried retrograde P wave
Correct. In the typical form, retrograde P waves are buried at the end of the QRS complex; these are called pseudo S waves.
A fibrillatory wave
Fibrillatory waves are chaotic baseline activity in atrial fibrillation, not a repeating notch on a regular rhythm.
C.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 39
C.alt: Rhythm strip of tall, evenly spaced narrow complexes; a yellow circle highlights the small notch at the end of each one.

C.io: Compare and contrast ECG manifestations of electrolyte abnormalities.
C.q: A 59-year-old man with untreated kidney failure has the 12-lead shown: very wide QRS complexes, no P waves and peaked T waves. Without treatment, which pattern comes next?
opts: Prominent U waves
Prominent U waves are a hypokalemia sign, the opposite disturbance.
A sine wave
Correct. Hyperkalemia progresses from peaked T waves to flattened P waves and a wide QRS, and finally to a sine wave, the end-stage pattern.
A shortened QT interval
A shortened QTc with the T wave against the QRS is the hypercalcemia pattern.
Osborn waves
Osborn waves are terminal QRS notches of hypothermia, not the end stage of hyperkalemia.

C.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
C.q: A 61-year-old woman's 12-lead has a good general impression and standard calibration. What is assessed next?
opts: The ST segments
ST and T wave changes come last in the systematic approach, after axis, QRS and hypertrophy.
Hypertrophy
Hypertrophy and chamber enlargement come after the axis and the QRS assessment.
The axis
Correct. The systematic approach runs: general impression, calibration, axis, QRS assessment, hypertrophy and chamber enlargement, then ST and T wave changes.
Bundle branch blocks
Bundle branch blocks belong to the QRS assessment, which follows the axis.

C.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
C.q: A 78-year-old man has this electrocardiogram. What do its lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6) lack?
opts: Q waves
Correct. In left bundle branch block the septal fascicle is blocked, so the septum's normal Q wave is lost from the lateral leads.
R waves
The lateral leads in left bundle branch block have tall, often notched R waves. It is the Q wave that is missing.
T waves
T waves are present after each complex. The missing wave is the septal Q wave.
P waves
P waves are atrial and appear across the leads in sinus rhythm. The lateral leads lack Q waves.

C.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
C.q: A 47-year-old man's strip shows an early narrow beat. Which feature marks it as a premature atrial complex?
opts: No P wave and a wide QRS
A wide early beat with no P wave is a premature ventricular complex.
An inverted P with short PR
An inverted P wave with a short PR points to the atrioventricular junction, a premature junctional complex.
An early P wave of new shape
Correct. Premature atrial complexes arrive early in the cardiac cycle with P waves of different morphology, followed by a narrow QRS.
A late beat after a pause
A late beat after a pause is an escape beat; a premature atrial complex arrives early.
C.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 6

C.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
C.q: A 73-year-old man is found diaphoretic, and the monitor shows this rhythm. What is it?
opts: Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
The polymorphic form is irregular and its complexes change shape and twist. These complexes are identical from beat to beat.
Coarse ventricular fibrillation
Ventricular fibrillation, coarse or fine, is chaotic, with no measurable QRS. This rhythm is perfectly organized.
Atrial and ventricular pacing
Dual pacing shows a spike before the P wave and another before each QRS. There are no pacer spikes on this strip.
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
Correct. Large, regular complexes of one identical shape with no P waves are monomorphic ventricular tachycardia.
C.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 5
C.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

C.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
C.q: A 74-year-old man has this electrocardiogram. Which conduction abnormality does it show?
opts: Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block makes V1 end negative and notches the lateral leads without slurred S waves.
Left anterior fascicular block
Left anterior fascicular block is a narrow-QRS block with left axis deviation. These complexes are wide.
Right bundle branch block
Correct. The QRS is wide, V1 shows an rSR pattern ending in a positive deflection, and the lateral leads carry slurred S waves: right bundle branch block.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy raises voltage with a normal duration. These complexes are wide with an rSR in V1.
C.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 48
C.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

C.io: Compare and contrast sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
C.q: A 76-year-old man has a regular rate of 52 per minute (normal 60 to 100) with wide QRS complexes. What still makes the rhythm sinus?
opts: The slow ventricular rate
Rate separates bradycardia from tachycardia but does not prove a sinus origin; married normal P waves do.
The regular R to R
Junctional and ventricular rhythms are regular too; the sinus origin shows in normal P waves married to each QRS.
Married normal P waves
Correct. What makes a rhythm sinus is normal P waves present and married to the QRS complexes; sinus bradycardia and tachycardia may have narrow or wide QRS.
The wide QRS complexes
A wide QRS reflects abnormal ventricular conduction, not the pacemaker; married normal P waves make it sinus.
C.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 75, 78

C.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
C.q: A 49-year-old man has ST elevation in I and aVL with reciprocal depression in III and aVF. Which region is infarcting?
opts: Inferior wall
The inferior leads III and aVF are depressed here, the reciprocal of a high lateral infarction.
Anteroseptal wall
The anteroseptal wall is viewed by V1 to V4, which are not the leads elevated here.
Posterior wall
The posterior wall shows as isolated depression in V1 to V4 with no elevation anywhere.
High lateral wall
Correct. I and aVL are contiguous leads looking at the high lateral wall of the left ventricle, with reciprocal ST depression in the inferior leads III and aVF.
C.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 17

C.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
C.q: A 31-year-old woman has global concave ST elevation. Her lead V6 is shown, with the ST elevation boxed in blue and the T-wave height in red. Which diagnosis does the ratio favor?
opts: Benign early repolarization
Early repolarization gives a V6 ST/T ratio under 25%, with much more T wave than ST elevation; this ratio is higher.
Brugada syndrome
Brugada changes are isolated to V1 to V3; the V6 ratio separates pericarditis from early repolarization.
Hypercalcemia
Hypercalcemia shortens the ST segment until the T wave sits against the QRS; it does not raise the ST/T ratio.
Acute pericarditis
Correct. The ST elevation is about half the T-wave height. An ST/T ratio above 25% in V6 suggests pericarditis: more ST elevation than T wave (the V6 phenomenon).
C.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 9
C.alt: Lead V6 rhythm strip with a blue box and a red box drawn over one beat

C.io: Correlate ECG findings with clinical implications of ventricular arrhythmias and AV blocks
C.q: A 78-year-old man's monitor shows this. What is his cardiac output?
opts: None, although the atria contract
Correct. This is ventricular standstill: atrial contractions with no ventricular contractions, so there is no detectable pulse and no cardiac output.
Normal, because the atria contract
Atrial contraction alone does not pump blood to the body. With no ventricular contraction there is no output.
Reduced, from a slow escape rhythm
A slow escape rhythm would show QRS complexes. There are none here, so there is no ventricular output.
Normal if the P waves are regular
Regular P waves show only that the atria are firing. The ventricles are not contracting, so there is no output.
C.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 17
C.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

C.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
C.q: A 31-year-old man's V1 to V3 show convex, coved ST elevation. Which Brugada type is this?
opts: Type 2
Type 2 Brugada is the saddle-shaped ST elevation (carousel horses sign), not coved.
Type A
Types A and B are Wolff-Parkinson-White pathways (left or right Kent bundle), not Brugada patterns.
Type 1
Correct. Type 1 Brugada is convex ST elevation in V1 to V3, also called the coved-shaped type.
Type B
Type B is a right-sided Kent bundle in Wolff-Parkinson-White, with a mostly negative QRS in V1.
C.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 10

C.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block Type I, second-degree AV block Type II, third-degree AV block
C.q: A 52-year-old woman is being evaluated for a conduction delay. Which hallmark defines first-degree block?
opts: A PR that lengthens until a beat drops
Progressive PR lengthening with a dropped beat is second-degree type I. First-degree block has no dropped beats.
Sinus rhythm with a PR beyond 0.2 seconds
Correct. The hallmark of first-degree block is a sinus rhythm having a PR interval beyond 0.2 seconds in duration.
A constant PR with some dropped beats
A constant PR with dropped QRS complexes is second-degree type II. First-degree block drops nothing.
P waves unrelated to the QRS complexes
P waves unrelated to the QRS complexes are third-degree block. In first-degree block each P wave is married to its QRS.
C.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 23

C.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement: left atrial enlargement, right atrial enlargement
C.q: A 68-year-old woman with mitral valve disease has this V1. What do its P waves show?
opts: Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement makes the V1 P wave's positive first part the larger one. Here the negative terminal part dominates.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy shows more R wave than S wave in V1. The marked finding here is the P wave.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS voltage finding. The marked finding here is the P wave.
Left atrial enlargement
Correct. A biphasic P wave in V1 with a small positive start and a large negative terminal deflection is P mitrale: left atrial enlargement.
C.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 31
C.alt: Lead V1 tracing with arrows marking the P waves

C.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: incomplete and complete right bundle branch block, incomplete and complete left bundle branch block
C.q: A 61-year-old woman is told her electrocardiogram shows bunny ears in V1. Why should that pattern not be relied on?
opts: Bunny ears mean left bundle block
Bunny ears are taught for the right side, and even there they are not reliable. The J point rule decides.
Bunny ears are a normal variant
The problem is not that bunny ears are normal; it is that right bundle branch block takes many V1 shapes besides them.
Bunny ears need a narrow QRS
Every bundle branch block has a wide QRS. The issue is that V1 morphology varies, while the J point rule does not.
Right bundle block has many V1 shapes
Correct. Right bundle branch block can have many morphologies in V1; the constant is that the first deflection back from the J point is positive.
C.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 17

C.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of AV nodal and infranodal conduction abnormalities
C.q: A 65-year-old man in ventricular fibrillation has no pulse. Why is there no pulse in this rhythm?
opts: The ventricles quiver, not contract
Correct. Chaotic firing leaves the heart muscle unable to contract, so it quivers; with no ventricular contraction there is no cardiac output and no pulse.
The atria stop firing completely
Atrial activity is not what fails. In ventricular fibrillation the ventricles quiver and never contract, which is why output stops.
The QRS complexes are too wide
There are no measurable QRS complexes in ventricular fibrillation. The pulse is absent because the ventricles do not contract.
The sinoatrial node is blocked
A sinoatrial block would not stop the ventricles quivering. The problem is chaotic ventricular firing with no contraction.
C.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 12

C.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block, third-degree AV block
C.q: A 70-year-old man has second-degree type II block. Which statement about his dropped beats is correct?
opts: Only one ever drops at a time
Type II can drop more than one beat in a row; that is part of why it is the more serious second-degree block.
Beats drop after the PR lengthens
Dropping after progressive PR lengthening is second-degree type I. In type II the PR stays constant.
More than one may drop in a row
Correct. In second-degree type II it is possible to have more than one dropped beat in a row.
No beats drop; only the PR is long
A long PR with no dropped beats is first-degree block. Type II drops QRS complexes.
C.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 35

C.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes
C.q: A 66-year-old woman's monitor shows a regular rhythm with a P wave before each QRS, but she has no pulse. What does this combination represent?
opts: Mechanical activity without electrical activity
Contraction needs depolarization first, so this combination does not occur. The monitor shows electricity; the muscle is not producing a pulse.
Electrical activity without mechanical activity
Correct. Pulseless electrical activity is organized electrical activity on the monitor with no mechanical activity, so there is no pulse.
Atrial activity without ventricular activity
That is ventricular standstill, with P waves and no QRS. This monitor shows QRS complexes after every P wave.
No electrical or mechanical activity
That is asystole, a flat line. This monitor shows organized complexes.
C.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 16

C.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ventricular hypertrophy
C.q: A 70-year-old man with hypertension has ST elevation in V1 to V3 on this electrocardiogram. Which condition explains the pattern as a mimic?
opts: Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy shows more R than S wave in V1 and V2 with a strain pattern. Here V1 to V3 are deep S waves with concave elevation.
Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block gives an rSR in V1 with slurred lateral S waves, not huge voltages with concave elevation.
Left atrial enlargement
Left atrial enlargement is a P wave finding and does not elevate the ST segment.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Correct. Huge QRS voltages with concave, upward-sloping ST elevation in V1 to V3 and lateral T wave inversion are left ventricular hypertrophy, the most common mimic of ST-elevation infarction.
C.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 59
C.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

C.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
C.q: A 62-year-old man has ST elevation in lead I. Which lead is contiguous with lead I?
opts: aVF
aVF is an inferior lead, contiguous with II and III; it looks from the opposite direction to lead I.
aVL
Correct. I and aVL are contiguous leads that look at the high lateral wall of the left ventricle.
V1
V1 is a septal lead, contiguous with V2; it does not view the high lateral wall.
III
Lead III is inferior, contiguous with II and aVF, and is a reciprocal lead for a high lateral infarction.
C.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 17

C.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular escape rhythms
C.q: A 70-year-old man's rate is 50 per minute (normal 60 to 100); his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Junctional escape rhythm
Correct. A regular rhythm of 40 to 60 per minute with inverted P waves just before narrow QRS complexes and a short PR is a junctional escape rhythm.
Accelerated junctional rhythm
Accelerated junctional rhythm has the same look at 60 to 100 per minute; at 50 it is a junctional escape rhythm.
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia has upright P waves with a normal PR; inverted P waves with a short PR are junctional.
Idioventricular rhythm
Idioventricular rhythm is wide with no P waves at 20 to 40; these complexes are narrow.
C.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 54, 55, 56
C.alt: Rhythm strip with regularly spaced narrow complexes, each preceded closely by a small downward deflection.

C.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
C.q: A 71-year-old woman's strip is shown; her narrow-complex rhythm has no visible P waves. What explains their absence?
opts: The atria fire first
Atria firing first would leave an inverted P wave before the QRS; here there is none.
The sinus node is firing
A sinus-driven rhythm shows upright P waves; their absence points to a junctional impulse.
The impulse starts in the ventricle
A ventricular rhythm would be wide; these complexes are narrow, junctional with the P hidden.
Atria and ventricles fire together
Correct. When a junctional impulse depolarizes the atria and ventricles at the same time, the QRS hides the P wave (or the atria are never depolarized).
C.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 48
C.alt: Rhythm strip of regularly spaced narrow complexes, each followed by a rounded wave, with flat baseline and no wave before them.

C.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of myocardial ischemia and infarction.
C.q: A 64-year-old man with no known heart history has a complex like this in leads II, III and aVF. What does the deep first deflection represent?
opts: Death of myocardial tissue
Correct. Pathological Q waves represent infarction, the actual death of cardiac tissue, from either a previous or an acute cardiac event.
Reversible ischemia
Reversible ischemia shows as hyperacute T waves or ST depression. A pathologic Q wave means tissue has already died.
Transmural injury in progress
Injury (transmural ischemia) is shown by ST elevation. The Q wave marks infarction, the stage after injury.
Normal septal activation
A normal septal Q wave is small and shallow; one this deep, past 2 mm and a quarter of the R wave's height, meets the pathologic criteria.
C.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 12
C.alt: A single electrocardiogram complex on grid paper

C.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, SVT, atrial tachycardia
C.q: A 22-year-old marathon runner's rate is 190 per minute (normal 60 to 100), with an upright P wave before every QRS. What is the rhythm?
opts: Supraventricular tachycardia
The reentry tachycardia called supraventricular tachycardia has no visible P waves (or retrograde ones); upright P before each QRS is sinus.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia needs P waves of three shapes and is irregular; one upright P shape is sinus.
Junctional tachycardia
Junctional tachycardia has inverted, hidden or retrograde P waves; an upright P before each QRS is sinus.
Sinus tachycardia
Correct. The rate does not determine the rhythm: normal P waves married to every QRS make it sinus, so this is sinus tachycardia, even at 190.
C.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 40

C.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: digoxin toxicity, amiodarone toxicity, tricyclic antidepressant toxicity
C.q: A 21-year-old woman took an overdose of a tricyclic antidepressant. Which pair of tracing changes does the overdose produce?
opts: QT shortening and bradycardia
Both go the wrong way: a tricyclic overdose prolongs the QT and speeds the heart through anticholinergic activity.
Peaked T waves and flat P waves
Peaked T waves with flattened P waves are the hyperkalemia progression, not a tricyclic overdose.
Delta waves and a short PR
A delta wave with a short PR interval is preexcitation through an accessory pathway, not a drug effect.
QT prolongation and tachycardia
Correct. A tricyclic overdose prolongs the QT and, through anticholinergic activity, speeds the heart; its fast sodium-channel blockade also widens the QRS.
C.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 49

C.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: Benign Early Repolarization (BER), acute pericarditis, long QT syndrome
C.q: A 24-year-old man's 12-lead is shown: concave ST elevation with notched J points and no reciprocal depression. What clinical significance does this pattern carry?
opts: It signals an evolving infarction
An infarction shows localized elevation with reciprocal depression; diffuse concave elevation with J waves and no reciprocal change is the benign variant.
It predicts sudden cardiac death
Arrhythmia risk belongs to Brugada syndrome, an inherited arrhythmogenic disease with V1 to V3 changes, not to benign early repolarization.
None; it is a normal variant
Correct. Benign early repolarization, also called normal variant ST elevation, is seen mostly in young men and has no clinical significance.
It indicates pericardial inflammation
Pericardial inflammation adds PR-segment depression; benign early repolarization has no clinical significance.
C.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 7; tracing from Slide 8
C.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

C.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
C.q: A 66-year-old woman's strip is shown, and its R to R intervals vary. Which rate method suits it best?
opts: The 1500 method
The 1500 method divides by the small boxes of a single R to R interval, so it misleads when intervals vary.
The 300 method
The 300 method divides by the large boxes of one R to R interval, so it misleads in an irregular rhythm.
The six-second method
Correct. The six-second method counts every complex across six seconds, so it still works when R to R intervals vary; the box-counting methods use a single interval.
The count-down method
Counting down heavy lines from one R wave to the next reads only one interval and is unreliable when they vary.
C.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 44, 48, 52
C.alt: Rhythm strip with narrow complexes whose spacing varies noticeably from one beat to the next.

C.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
C.q: A 61-year-old woman's strip is shown; her PR intervals fall outside the normal 0.12 to 0.20 seconds. Which can cause this?
opts: Atrioventricular nodal block
Correct. Atrioventricular nodal blocks, accessory pathways and alternate pacemaker sites within the heart can put the PR interval outside its normal range.
Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus arrhythmia varies the R to R interval with breathing but keeps a normal PR; blocks, accessory pathways and alternate pacemakers change the PR.
Sinus tachycardia at rest
Sinus tachycardia raises the rate with a normal PR interval; an atrioventricular nodal block can move it outside the range.
Normal sinus rhythm
Normal sinus rhythm by definition has a constant PR of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds; nodal blocks change it.
C.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 59
C.alt: Lead II strip with brackets under the PR intervals of successive beats and one P wave labeled on its own.

C.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
C.q: A 39-year-old man's tracing shows a tall deflection. On electrocardiogram paper, what does the vertical axis measure?
opts: Voltage
Correct. Up and down on the paper measures voltage; moving left to right measures time.
Time
Time runs along the horizontal axis, left to right; the vertical axis is voltage.
Heart rate
Heart rate is worked out from intervals along the time axis; the vertical axis is voltage.
Paper speed
Paper speed is fixed at 25 millimeters per second along the horizontal axis; height is voltage.
C.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 26

C.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
C.q: A 63-year-old man's strip is shown. What is the early beat?
opts: Premature atrial complex
A premature atrial complex is narrow with its own early P wave; this beat is wide with no P wave.
Premature junctional complex
A premature junctional complex is narrow; this early beat is wide and deep.
Ventricular escape complex
A ventricular escape complex is wide but late, after a pause; this one comes early.
Premature ventricular complex
Correct. The early beat is wide and bizarre, with no P wave, and its T wave points opposite to the QRS: a premature ventricular complex.
C.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 69, 70
C.alt: Pink grid strip of narrow complexes with small rounded waves; one early beat is a deep, broad downward complex followed by an upright wave.

C.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
C.q: A 57-year-old man has chest pain and the 12-lead shown, with ST elevation in V1 to V3. Occlusion of which artery best explains it?
opts: Right coronary artery
The right coronary artery supplies the right heart and the bottom of the left ventricle; its occlusion elevates II, III and aVF, which are depressed here.
Left circumflex artery
The circumflex supplies the left atrium and the side and back of the left ventricle; it does not explain elevation in V1 to V3.
Left anterior descending
Correct. The left anterior descending artery supplies the front of the left ventricle and the front of the septum, the anterior and septal walls that V1 to V3 face.
A coronary vein
The coronary veins return used blood to the right atrium; an infarction pattern comes from an arterial occlusion.
C.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 4; tracing from Slide 18
C.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

C.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
C.q: A 57-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram. What is her electrical axis?
opts: Left axis deviation
Correct. Lead I is mostly positive (up) and aVF is mostly negative (down): left axis deviation.
Normal axis
A normal axis has a mostly positive QRS in both lead I and aVF; the normal range is -30 to +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation has lead I mostly negative and aVF mostly positive, an axis beyond +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Extreme axis deviation
Extreme axis deviation, no man's land, has both lead I and aVF mostly negative. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
C.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 50
C.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

C.io: Recognize common supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation
C.q: A 71-year-old woman's strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Supraventricular tachycardia
The reentry tachycardia called supraventricular tachycardia has no visible atrial waves; this baseline is a sawtooth of flutter waves.
Atrial flutter
Correct. Regularly spaced narrow complexes ride on a repeating pointed sawtooth baseline (flutter waves at an atrial rate of about 300): atrial flutter.
Atrial fibrillation
Fibrillation is irregularly irregular with a disorganized baseline; this strip is regular with an organized sawtooth.
Junctional tachycardia
Junctional tachycardia has a single inverted P wave per QRS; here several flutter waves fill each interval.
C.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 27, 28, 29
C.alt: Long rhythm strip of narrow spikes with a repeating pointed zigzag baseline between them, the spikes evenly spaced.

C.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction.
C.q: A healthy 30-year-old woman has the rhythm strip shown. Which description fits her T waves?
opts: Broad, tall and symmetrical
Broad, tall, symmetrical T waves are hyperacute T waves, the earliest sign of ischemia; normal T waves are asymmetrical.
Inverted below the baseline
These T waves are upright. T-wave inversion is an ischemic sign, not the normal shape.
Asymmetrical, slow upstroke
Correct. Normal T waves are asymmetrical, with a slow initial upstroke and a sharper negative terminal deflection, and a modest amplitude.
Peaked and narrow
Peaked, symmetric T waves are the early sign of hyperkalemia. A normal T wave rises slowly and falls more sharply.
C.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 7
C.alt: A single-lead rhythm strip on grid paper

C.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
C.q: A 79-year-old woman has lost both sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodal function. Which structure now paces her heart?
opts: Bundle of His
The bundle of His conducts the impulse from the atrioventricular node to the bundle branches; the third pacemaker is the Purkinje network.
Bachmann's bundle
Bachmann's bundle is the main route of conduction between the atria; it is not the backup to the two nodes.
Middle internodal tract
The internodal tracts connect the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes; the pacemaker after both nodes is the Purkinje network.
Purkinje network
Correct. The Purkinje network is the heart's third pacemaker, taking over when both nodes fail, at 20 to 40 per minute.
C.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 14, 15

C.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
C.q: A 64-year-old man has palpitations and a palpable pulse. His monitor shows this rhythm. What is it?
opts: Torsades de pointes
Torsades de pointes is polymorphic: the complexes change shape and twist around the baseline. Every complex here has the same shape.
Ventricular fibrillation
Ventricular fibrillation has no measurable QRS complexes, only chaotic waves at 300 to 500 per minute. These complexes are organized and identical.
Ventricular tachycardia
Correct. Regular, wide, identical complexes at a fast rate with no P waves are ventricular tachycardia; this example runs at 140 per minute.
Ventricular paced rhythm
A ventricular paced rhythm puts a pacer spike before every wide QRS. No spikes precede these complexes, so a ventricular focus is driving them.
C.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 8
C.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

C.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
C.q: A 68-year-old man's lead II strip is shown. What pattern do the wide premature beats follow?
opts: Bigeminy
Bigeminy is a premature beat every other beat; here three normal beats separate the wide ones.
Quadrigeminy
Correct. Every fourth beat is a wide premature complex, three normal beats then an early one: quadrigeminy (here ventricular).
Trigeminy
Trigeminy is every third beat premature; here it is every fourth.
A couplet
A couplet is two wide beats back to back; here each wide beat stands alone, every fourth beat.
C.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 10, 73
C.alt: Lead II strip with narrow complexes and, at regular intervals, a single broad deep complex after every three narrow ones.

C.io: Recognize sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia
C.q: A 68-year-old man feels tired; his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Normal sinus rhythm
Normal sinus rhythm runs 60 to 100 per minute; R waves here are about six large boxes apart, just over 50.
Sinus pause
A sinus pause breaks an otherwise steady rhythm with one gap; here every R to R interval is the same, just long.
Sinus bradycardia
Correct. The rhythm is regular and slow, about 51 per minute, with normal P waves married to narrow QRS complexes and a normal PR interval.
Sinus exit block
Sinus exit block drops a cycle and leaves a gap; this strip is regular, merely slow.
C.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 75, 77
C.alt: Rhythm strip with three widely spaced narrow complexes, each preceded by a small upright wave, at equal intervals.

C.io: Apply a systematic approach to ECG interpretation
C.q: A 45-year-old man's strip has been assessed for rate, regularity, P waves and PR interval. What is the final step?
opts: The rate
Rate is the first step, not the last; the systematic approach ends with the QRS.
The QRS
Correct. The five steps are rate, regularity, P waves, PR interval and QRS; the QRS (narrow under 0.12 seconds, or wide) comes last.
The T wave
The T wave is not one of the five systematic steps; the approach ends with the QRS.
The axis
Axis belongs to 12-lead interpretation; the five rhythm steps end with the QRS.
C.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 42

C.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of AV nodal and infranodal conduction abnormalities
C.q: An 80-year-old man has this paced strip. Why are the QRS complexes wide?
opts: The atrioventricular node is blocked
The width does not come from a nodal block. It comes from the beat starting in the ventricle, where the pacemaker lead fires.
The ventricles are paced below the atria
Correct. Ventricular pacemakers pace the ventricles below the level of the atria, so the impulse spreads outside the normal pathway and the QRS is wide.
Many ventricular foci fire at once
Chaotic firing of many foci is ventricular fibrillation. Here one paced focus fires on schedule after each spike.
The atria are being paced
Atrial pacing gives a normal, narrow QRS through the normal pathway. A wide QRS after a spike means the ventricle is paced.
C.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 18
C.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

C.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
C.q: A 20-year-old woman's 12-lead is shown. What is the slurred upstroke at the start of each QRS called?
opts: A J wave
A J (Osborn) wave is a notch at the end of the QRS, in hypothermia and early repolarization.
A delta wave
Correct. The delta wave is a slurring of the QRS upstroke: impulses bypass the atrioventricular node through the accessory pathway and begin depolarizing the ventricles early.
A U wave
A U wave follows the T wave and is prominent in hypokalemia.
A pacing spike
A pacing spike is a sharp vertical artifact before a paced QRS, not a gradual slur.
C.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 27; tracing from Slide 29
C.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

C.io: Review ECG lead placement
C.q: A 62-year-old woman's septal wall is in question. Which leads look at the septum?
opts: V1 and V2
Correct. V1 and V2 look at the septal wall; V3 and V4 look at the anterior wall beside it.
V3 and V4
V3 and V4 look at the anterior wall of the left ventricle; the septum is V1 and V2.
V5 and V6
V5 and V6 join I and aVL (augmented vector left) on the lateral wall; the septum is V1 and V2.
II and III
Leads II and III join aVF (augmented vector foot) on the inferior wall; the septum is V1 and V2.
C.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 69

C.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
C.q: A 70-year-old man has chest pain, hypotension, clear lungs and distended neck veins. His 12-lead is shown. Which is the next best step?
opts: Record posterior leads V7 to V9
Posterior leads answer isolated ST depression in V1 to V4. Hypotension, clear lungs and distended neck veins with an inferior infarct point to the right ventricle.
Repeat the standard 12 leads only
The standard 12-lead does not look at the right ventricle in its entirety; only a right-sided lead such as V4R can confirm its involvement.
No more leads; it is inferior only
Hypotension, clear lungs and jugular vein distension in an inferior infarction are the cue to suspect right ventricular involvement, so it cannot be assumed inferior only.
Record right-sided lead V4R

Correct. This is an inferior ST-elevation infarction, and hypotension with clear lungs and jugular vein distension raises suspicion of right ventricular involvement. Moving V4 to the right (V4R) rules it in or out.
C.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 22; tracing from Slide 23
C.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

C.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
C.q: A 45-year-old man's tracing is being measured for ST changes. Where is the J point?
opts: Where the T wave ends
The end of the T wave marks the end of repolarization. The J point is the junction at the end of the QRS.
Where the P wave begins
The start of the P wave is atrial depolarization; the J point sits at the end of the QRS complex.
End of the QRS, start of ST
Correct. The junction point, or J point, lies between the QRS complex and the ST segment; ST deviation is judged at this point.
At the peak of the R wave
The R-wave peak is within the QRS; the J point is where the QRS ends and the ST segment begins.
C.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 5

C.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
C.q: A 66-year-old man is told his blocked artery supplies the left atrium and the side and back of the left ventricle. Which artery is it?
opts: Right coronary artery
The right coronary artery supplies the right atrium, right ventricle, bottom of the left ventricle and back of the septum.
Left circumflex artery
Correct. The circumflex artery supplies blood to the left atrium and the side and back of the left ventricle, the lateral and posterior walls.
Left anterior descending
The left anterior descending artery supplies the front of the left ventricle and the front of the septum.
Pulmonary artery
The pulmonary artery carries blood to the lungs; it does not supply the myocardium. The coronary arteries do.
C.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 4

C.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
C.q: A 74-year-old woman with chest pain has a left bundle branch block. Why are Sgarbossa's criteria needed?
opts: The block itself distorts the ST segment

Correct. Left bundle branch blocks and ventricular paced rhythms cause global ST elevation, T-wave changes and wide QRS complexes, so ordinary criteria cannot locate an infarction; Sgarbossa's criteria are used instead.
The block lowers the troponin
The criteria answer an electrocardiographic problem, the distorted ST segment, not a laboratory one.
The block makes the rate too fast
Rate is not the problem; the widened QRS with global ST and T changes is.
Standard leads cannot be placed
All twelve leads are recorded normally; it is the block's own ST and T changes that hide an infarction.
C.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 13

C.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: COPD/COLD, pulmonary embolism, hypothermia
C.q: A 58-year-old man has a large pulmonary embolism. Which axis change does his tracing tend to show?
opts: A rightward axis shift
Correct. Dilation and enlargement of the right ventricle under high pressure causes more of a rightward axis deviation in pulmonary embolism.
A leftward axis shift
The strained, dilated chamber is the right ventricle, which pulls the axis rightward.
No axis change is possible
Right ventricular dilation does shift the axis, toward the right.
An axis that alternates beats
Alternating beats suggest bigeminy (as in digoxin toxicity), not a pulmonary embolism axis change.
C.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 50

C.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: myocardial ischemia, myocardial injury, myocardial infarction
C.q: A 61-year-old man has myocardial ischemia from an acute coronary syndrome. How can this move his J point?
opts: Only above the baseline
Ischemia can push the J point either way: below the baseline as ST depression (subendocardial) or above it as ST elevation (transmural).
Only below the baseline
Ischemia can also raise the J point, as ST elevation from transmural ischemia. Both directions occur.
It never moves the J point
J-point displacement is exactly how ischemia shows on the tracing, as ST elevation or ST depression.
Above or below the baseline
Correct. Cardiac events such as myocardial ischemia (acute coronary syndrome) can cause depression or elevation of the J point relative to the baseline, called ST elevation or ST depression.
C.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 5

D.io: Recognize common pacemaker rhythms and pacing artifacts.
D.q: An 81-year-old woman has the 12-lead shown. Which rhythm is it?
opts: Left bundle branch block
A left bundle branch block also gives wide QRS complexes and global ST and T changes, but there is no pacing spike before each complex.
Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia is a fast wide-complex rhythm without pacing spikes; this rate is not fast and every beat is preceded by a spike.
Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern
