Wolff-Parkinson-White shows a short PR interval and a slurred delta wave, not a pacing spike before each QRS.
Ventricular paced rhythm
Correct. A sharp pacing spike before each wide QRS, with T waves pointing opposite the QRS (contralateral T waves) and global ST changes, is a ventricular paced rhythm.
D.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 14
D.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

D.io: Compare and contrast sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
D.q: A 57-year-old woman asks how normal sinus rhythm, sinus bradycardia and sinus tachycardia differ. What separates them?
opts: The P wave shape
All three share normal, uniform P waves from the sinoatrial node; only the rate separates them.
The rate alone
Correct. All three are regular with normal P waves married to the QRS and a normal PR; only the ventricular rate (under 60, 60 to 100, over 100) differs.
The PR interval
All three keep a normal PR of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds; the rate is what differs.
The regularity
All three are regular; irregularity with sinus P waves is sinus arrhythmia.
D.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 72, 75, 78

D.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of supraventricular arrhythmias
D.q: A 79-year-old woman's atria are fibrillating. What does she lose?
opts: All ventricular filling
Seventy to 80 percent of ventricular filling is passive and continues; what is lost is the atrial kick.
Ventricular contraction
The ventricles still contract, at an irregular rate; what fibrillating atria lose is their own kick.
The atrial kick
Correct. In atrial fibrillation the atria quiver rather than contract, so the atrial kick (contraction) is lost; most ventricular filling is passive and continues.
Atrioventricular conduction
Impulses still reach the ventricles irregularly through the node; the lost function is the atrial kick.
D.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 32

D.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block Type I, second-degree AV block Type II, third-degree AV block
D.q: A 76-year-old man with a recent inferior infarction has this strip. What is the rhythm?
opts: Third-degree (complete) block
Correct. The P waves march at their own regular rate and the narrow QRS complexes beat regularly at a slower rate, with no fixed PR: complete heart block.
Second-degree type I (Wenckebach)
Type I PR intervals lengthen in a predictable pattern before a single dropped beat. These PR intervals bear no relation to each other.
Second-degree type II (Mobitz II)
Type II has a constant PR on every conducted beat. Here no two PR intervals are the same.
First-degree atrioventricular block
First-degree block has one QRS per P wave at a long but fixed PR. Here there are more P waves than QRS complexes.
D.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 48
D.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

D.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: myocardial ischemia, myocardial injury, myocardial infarction
D.q: A healthy 30-year-old woman's T waves are shown. If ischemia began, which change in these T waves is often the very first sign?
opts: They become inverted
T-wave inversion is a sign of ischemia, but it comes later than hyperacute T waves.
They become flattened
Flattened T waves belong to hypokalemia and hypothyroidism, not to the first minutes of ischemia.
They become hyperacute
Correct. Hyperacute T waves, broad, increased in amplitude and symmetrical, are often the very first sign of cardiac ischemia; the normal T wave shown is asymmetrical.
They disappear entirely
The T wave does not vanish with ischemia; the earliest change is that it grows broad, tall and symmetrical.
D.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 7
D.alt: A single-lead rhythm strip on grid paper

D.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
D.q: A 62-year-old woman with a left bundle branch block has chest pain; her 12-lead is shown. How much discordant ST elevation meets Sgarbossa's criteria?
opts: 1 mm or more
One millimeter is the threshold for concordant elevation; discordant elevation must reach 5 mm or more.
5 mm or more
Correct. Discordant ST elevation of 5 mm or more in any lead with a negative QRS complex is a Sgarbossa criterion; smaller discordant elevation can be expected in the block.
2 mm or more
Two millimeters of discordant elevation is within what a left bundle branch block can produce; the criterion is 5 mm or more.
Any amount at all
Some discordant elevation is normal for a left bundle branch block, so a threshold of 5 mm or more is used.
D.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 18; tracing from Slide 19
D.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

D.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of myocardial ischemia and infarction.
D.q: A 71-year-old man with exertional chest pain has the 12-lead shown. Which layer of the heart does this pattern indicate is ischemic?
opts: The full wall thickness
Ischemia through the full wall thickness is transmural ischemia, also called injury, and it produces ST-segment elevation rather than depression.
The epicardium alone
The epicardium lies next to the coronary arteries and is the best perfused layer. Subendocardial ischemia, shown as ST depression, affects the innermost layer.
The pericardium
Inflammation of the pericardium (pericarditis) gives global concave ST elevation with PR depression, not the diffuse ST depression shown here.
The subendocardium
Correct. Global ST-segment depression represents subendocardial ischemia: the innermost layer, farthest from the epicardial coronary arteries, is starved first.
D.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 8; tracing from Slide 9
D.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

D.io: Define: normal axis, left axis deviation, right axis deviation
D.q: A 6-year-old boy has right axis deviation on a preoperative electrocardiogram. How should it be read?
opts: It can be normal in children
Correct. Right axis deviation is listed as normal in children.
It always signals heart disease
Right axis deviation is listed as a normal finding in children, so in a child it does not by itself signal disease.
It means a left fascicle is blocked
A left posterior fascicular block can cause right axis deviation, but in a child the axis can simply be normal.
It is caused by lead misplacement
Reversed arm leads can cause it, but right axis deviation is also a normal finding in children.
D.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 21

D.io: Recognize common supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation
D.q: A 77-year-old man's rate is 150 per minute (normal 60 to 100); his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia is regular with one sinus P wave shape; here the rhythm is irregular and the P waves vary.
Atrial flutter
Atrial flutter shows a regular sawtooth baseline instead of P waves; here separate P waves of differing shapes appear.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Correct. An irregular rhythm over 100 per minute with P waves of at least three shapes married to narrow complexes is multifocal atrial tachycardia.
Wandering atrial pacemaker
A wandering atrial pacemaker is the same rhythm under 100 per minute; at 150 it is multifocal atrial tachycardia.
D.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 17, 18, 21, 22
D.alt: Small lead II strip of very rapid narrow complexes at uneven spacing with small waves of varying shape between them.

D.io: Discuss related anatomy and physiology of ventricular conduction abnormalities and chamber enlargement
D.q: A 72-year-old woman has a bundle branch block with a double-humped QRS. What produces this two-QRS-complex phenomenon?
opts: Ventricles depolarizing in sequence
Correct. Because the ventricles are contracted in sequence rather than at the same time, the QRS shows two humps: the two QRS complex phenomenon.
Two separate pacemakers firing
Two independent pacemakers describe third-degree block. In a bundle branch block one impulse reaches the ventricles at different times.
Atrial and ventricular overlap
The P wave is not fused into the QRS here. The two humps come from the two ventricles depolarizing one after the other.
A pacer spike before each QRS
A pacer spike is a device artifact. The double QRS comes from sequential ventricular depolarization.
D.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 15

D.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
D.q: A 74-year-old woman's rate is 50 per minute (normal 60 to 100); her strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Idioventricular rhythm
Idioventricular rhythm also lacks P waves, but its complexes are wide and its rate is 20 to 40.
Junctional escape rhythm
Correct. A regular narrow-complex rhythm of 40 to 60 per minute with no visible P waves is a junctional escape rhythm; the P waves are hidden or absent.
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia would show an upright P wave before each QRS; here there are none.
Junctional tachycardia
Junctional tachycardia is the same pattern over 100 per minute; at 50 it is an escape rhythm.
D.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 54, 57, 58
D.alt: Rhythm strip on dark grid paper with regularly spaced narrow complexes and no wave in front of them.

D.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement: left atrial enlargement, right atrial enlargement
D.q: A 52-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram with right axis deviation. Which chamber finding do its P waves show?
opts: Left atrial enlargement
Left atrial enlargement gives humped, wide limb-lead P waves and a large negative terminal P in V1. These P waves are tall and peaked.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy would show more R wave than S wave in V1 and V2. The finding here is in the P waves.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS voltage finding with left axis deviation. This tracing has right axis deviation and peaked P waves.
Right atrial enlargement
Correct. The limb-lead P waves are tall and peaked and V1 shows a biphasic P with a larger positive first part: right atrial enlargement.
D.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 56
D.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

D.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
D.q: A 55-year-old woman's electrocardiogram needs a quick axis determination. Which two leads are used?
opts: Leads II and III
Leads II and III add detail, but the quick method uses lead I and aVF.
Leads V1 and V6
V1 and V6 are precordial leads used for bundle branch block morphology, not for the frontal axis.
Lead I and aVF
Correct. Leads I and aVF are used to quickly determine the axis: they sit at either end of the normal sector.
Leads aVR and aVL
The quick method uses lead I and aVF. aVR and aVL are not the pair it relies on.
D.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 22

D.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
D.q: A 62-year-old woman's posterior tracing has been recorded. Which finding confirms a posterior wall infarction?
opts: ST depression in V7 to V9
Depression is what the FRONT leads show; facing the infarct from behind, the posterior leads show elevation.
ST elevation in V7 to V9
Correct. ST-segment elevation in the posterior leads V7, V8 and V9 is the confirmatory sign of a posterior wall infarction.
Q waves in V1 and V2
Q waves in V1 and V2 would point to septal tissue death, not confirm a posterior infarction.
Hyperacute T waves in V5
A lateral lead's T waves do not confirm the posterior wall; the confirmation is elevation in V7 to V9.
D.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 19

D.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block Type I, second-degree AV block Type II, third-degree AV block
D.q: A 58-year-old man has this strip. What does the PR interval do across each group of beats?
opts: It stays constant, then a beat drops
A constant PR before a dropped beat is second-degree type II. Here the PR grows with each beat.
It lengthens until a beat drops
Correct. In Wenckebach the PR interval prolongs progressively until a P wave is not conducted; the dropped QRS resets the cycle.
It varies at random
A PR that varies with no pattern is third-degree block. This PR changes in a predictable, progressive way.
It is long but never changes
A long, unchanging PR with no dropped beats is first-degree block. This strip drops a beat after the PR grows.
D.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 32
D.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

D.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
D.q: A 66-year-old woman's strip is shown; every wide premature beat has the same shape. What does the matching shape indicate?
opts: One ectopic focus
Correct. Premature ventricular complexes with the same morphology are unifocal, coming from the same ectopic focus.
Several ectopic foci
Several foci produce premature ventricular complexes of differing shapes, which is multifocal.
An atrial origin
An atrial beat is narrow with its own P wave; these wide beats are ventricular, all from one focus.
A junctional origin
A junctional beat is narrow; matching wide beats come from a single ventricular focus.
D.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 70, 71
D.alt: Strip of narrow beats interrupted twice by runs of tall broad complexes that all look alike, a run of four and a run of three.

D.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of AV nodal and infranodal conduction abnormalities
D.q: A 69-year-old man is told he has an atrioventricular heart block. What does that term describe?
opts: Chaotic firing of ventricular foci
Chaotic firing of many ventricular foci is ventricular fibrillation. A heart block is a conduction delay or failure between atria and ventricles.
Failure of the sinoatrial node to fire
In the heart blocks the atria keep firing; P waves are present. The problem is getting the atrial impulse through to the ventricles.
A rapid rhythm from the ventricles
A rapid ventricular rhythm is ventricular tachycardia. A heart block is about conduction from the atria to the ventricles.
Delayed or failed atrioventricular conduction
Correct. Atrioventricular junction blocks are a delay in, or a complete failure of, the conduction of an atrial impulse through the atrioventricular node.
D.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 22

D.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
D.q: A 70-year-old woman has these limb leads with a narrow QRS. Which conduction abnormality do they show?
opts: Left anterior fascicular block
Left anterior fascicular block gives left axis deviation, lead I positive and aVF negative. Here lead I is negative.
Left posterior fascicular block
Correct. Right axis deviation (lead I mostly negative, aVF positive), an r wave in lead I with a q wave in lead III, and a positive lead III: left posterior fascicular block.
Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block is a wide-QRS block. These complexes are narrow.
Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block is wide, with an rSR pattern in V1. These complexes are narrow.
D.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 9
D.alt: Limb-lead tracings from an electrocardiogram

D.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
D.q: A 52-year-old man has crushing chest pain. His 12-lead is shown. Occlusion of which artery best explains the pattern in V1 to V4?
opts: Left anterior descending
Correct. ST elevation in V1 to V4 involves the septal and anterior walls, which the left anterior descending artery supplies (front of the left ventricle and front of the septum).
Right coronary artery
The right coronary artery supplies the right atrium, right ventricle and bottom of the left ventricle; its occlusion shows up in II, III and aVF, not V1 to V4.
Left circumflex artery
The circumflex supplies the side and back of the left ventricle; its territory shows in the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6) or as posterior changes.
A coronary vein
The coronary veins carry used, deoxygenated blood from the heart muscle back to the right atrium; an arterial occlusion causes this pattern.
D.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 11
D.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

D.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
D.q: A 20-year-old man is told he has preexcitation. What does the term mean?
opts: Early ventricular activation via a bypass

Correct. Preexcitation is activation of the ventricles by a supraventricular impulse earlier than normal, through an accessory pathway that connects atria to ventricles and bypasses the atrioventricular node.
Delayed conduction in the bundle branches
Delayed bundle branch conduction is a bundle branch block; preexcitation is early activation through an accessory pathway.
Early repolarization of the epicardium
That describes benign early repolarization, a repolarization variant, not preexcitation.
Atrial firing faster than the sinus node
Preexcitation is about the route to the ventricles, not the atrial rate.
D.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 25

D.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
D.q: A 63-year-old man asks how blood leaves the heart muscle once it has been used. Which vessels return it to the right atrium?
opts: The coronary arteries
The coronary arteries deliver oxygenated blood to the myocardium; it is the coronary veins that return the used blood.
The pulmonary arteries
The pulmonary arteries carry blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, not from the myocardium to the right atrium.
The coronary veins
Correct. The coronary veins take oxygen-poor blood that the heart muscle has already used and return it to the right atrium.
The vena cava
The vena cava returns blood from the body. The heart muscle's own used blood drains through the coronary veins.
D.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 4

D.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
D.q: A 79-year-old woman with a pacemaker has this strip. Which pacing does it show?
opts: Atrial and ventricular pacing
Correct. A spike precedes each P wave and another precedes every wide QRS: both chambers are being paced, which is rare.
Atrial pacing
Atrial pacing has one spike before the P wave and a normal, narrow QRS. These QRS complexes are wide and carry their own spike.
Ventricular pacing
Ventricular pacing has a spike before each QRS only. This strip also has a spike before each P wave.
Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia has no pacer spikes. Here two spikes start every cycle.
D.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 21
D.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

D.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: digoxin toxicity, amiodarone toxicity, tricyclic antidepressant toxicity
D.q: A 19-year-old man has the 12-lead shown after a tricyclic antidepressant overdose. Which interval change fits the overdose?
opts: A shortened QTc
A shortened QTc is the hypercalcemia pattern; tricyclic overdose prolongs the QT.
A short PR interval
A short PR interval with a delta wave is preexcitation through an accessory pathway.
QT prolongation
Correct. A tricyclic overdose prolongs the QT; its fast sodium-channel blockade also widens the QRS, as on this tracing, and its anticholinergic activity adds tachycardia.
A shortened ST segment
A shortened ST segment is the hypercalcemia finding, from a shortened phase 2.
D.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 49
D.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

D.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
D.q: A 68-year-old man has a Q wave in lead III. Which duration makes a Q wave pathologic?
opts: Longer than 0.02 seconds
Half a small box is too short a threshold. The pathologic duration is longer than 0.04 seconds, one small box.
Longer than 0.12 seconds
Three small boxes is a QRS width threshold, not the Q-wave criterion, which is longer than 0.04 seconds.
Longer than 0.20 seconds
One large box is the upper limit of the PR interval; a Q wave is pathologic when longer than 0.04 seconds.
Longer than 0.04 seconds
Correct. A pathological Q wave is longer than 0.04 seconds in duration, one small box, and deeper than 2 mm (or more than 25% of a following R wave).
D.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 12

D.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
D.q: A 72-year-old woman's rate is 65 per minute (normal 60 to 100); her strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Idioventricular rhythm
Idioventricular rhythm runs 20 to 40 per minute; at 65 the wide rhythm is accelerated.
Accelerated idioventricular rhythm
Correct. Regular wide complexes with no P waves at 65 per minute fall in the accelerated idioventricular range of 40 to 100.
Normal sinus rhythm
A sinus rhythm would have upright P waves married to each QRS; here the complexes are wide with no P waves.
Accelerated junctional rhythm
The accelerated junctional rhythm is usually narrow; wide complexes with no P waves are ventricular.
D.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 81, 84, 85
D.alt: Blue grid strip with regularly spaced broad complexes, each followed by an opposite-direction wave, nothing between them.

D.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
D.q: A 58-year-old man's strip is shown; the arrows mark two beats. What are the marked beats?
opts: Premature atrial complexes
A premature atrial complex has its own early P wave of new shape; the marked beats have none.
Premature ventricular complexes
A premature ventricular complex is wide; the marked beats are as narrow as the others.
Junctional escape beats
Junctional escape beats come late, after a pause; the marked beats arrive early.
Premature junctional complexes
Correct. Each marked beat comes early with a narrow QRS and no P wave in front of it: a premature junctional complex.
D.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 50
D.alt: Lead II rhythm strip of narrow complexes; two downward arrows mark beats that come sooner than expected with no wave just before them.

D.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: COPD/COLD, pulmonary embolism, hypothermia
D.q: A 70-year-old man with hypothermia has prominent Osborn waves. Which diagnosis are they frequently mistaken for?
opts: Wolff-Parkinson-White
Wolff-Parkinson-White has a delta wave at the start of the QRS; Osborn waves sit at its end and mimic ST elevation.
Hypokalemia
Hypokalemia's prominent U waves come after the T wave; Osborn waves are terminal QRS notches that look like ST elevation.
Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism gives low voltage and bradycardia; Osborn waves are mistaken for infarction.
ST-elevation infarction
Correct. Below 32°C (90°F) Osborn waves become apparent and are frequently mistaken for an ST-elevation infarction.
D.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 16

D.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes
D.q: A 72-year-old man in cardiac arrest has this rhythm. Which finding separates it from ventricular tachycardia?
opts: Absence of P waves
Neither rhythm shows P waves married to a QRS, so their absence does not separate the two.
No organized QRS complexes
Correct. This is ventricular fibrillation: chaotic waves with no measurable QRS. Ventricular tachycardia has organized, identical wide complexes.
A ventricular origin
Both rhythms come from the ventricles. The difference is a single organized focus versus chaotic firing of many foci.
A fast rate
Both are fast: 100 to 300 per minute for tachycardia, 300 to 500 for fibrillation. Organization is what separates them.
D.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 14
D.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

D.io: Compare and contrast ECG manifestations of electrolyte abnormalities.
D.q: A 64-year-old man has a serum sodium of 129 mEq/L (reference range 135 to 145). What change does this sodium level make to his tracing?
opts: Peaked T waves
Peaked T waves are the early sign of hyperkalemia, a potassium disturbance; sodium changes leave the tracing alone.
No change at all
Correct. Alterations in sodium levels do not cause any tracing or rhythm changes; it is potassium and calcium disturbances that change the tracing.
A prolonged QTc
A prolonged QTc with a long ST segment is a hypocalcemia finding; sodium changes do not alter the tracing.
Prominent U waves
Prominent U waves are a hypokalemia sign; altered sodium levels cause no tracing or rhythm change.
D.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 46

D.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
D.q: A 70-year-old woman's strip is assessed with R to R and P to P intervals. What are these intervals used for?
opts: QRS width and ST changes
QRS width is measured across the complex and ST changes against the TP baseline; the intervals give rate, regularity and blocks.
Lead placement and wiring
Placement is checked against the anatomical landmarks; the intervals assess rate, regularity and heart blocks.
Rate, regularity, heart blocks
Correct. R to R and P to P intervals are used to assess rhythm rate and regularity and also to assess heart blocks.
Axis and chamber enlargement
Axis comes from the limb leads; R to R and P to P intervals assess rate, regularity and heart blocks.
D.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 41

D.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
D.q: A 28-year-old man's 12-lead is shown, with ST elevation in V2. Which pattern is this?
opts: Type 1 Brugada (coved)
Type 1 is coved, convex elevation sloping straight down into the T wave; the saddle shape is type 2.
Type 2 Brugada (saddleback)
Correct. Saddle-shaped (saddleback) ST elevation in V1 to V3 is type 2 Brugada; type 1 is the coved, convex shape.
Acute pericarditis
Pericarditis elevates the ST segment globally with PR depression, not in a saddle shape confined to V1 to V3.
Hyperkalemia
Hyperkalemia shows peaked, symmetric T waves, then flattened P waves and a wide QRS; it has no saddle-shaped ST segment.
D.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 12
D.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

D.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
D.q: A 64-year-old man's QRS is 0.13 seconds (normal under 0.12). Which V1 pattern fits right bundle branch block?
opts: rS pattern
An rS pattern in V1, ending negative, is left bundle branch block.
QS pattern
A wholly negative complex in V1 ends negative, the left bundle branch block side.
Notched R in V6 only
A notched R in V6 is the left bundle branch block double QRS phenomenon, not a V1 pattern of the right side.
rSR pattern
Correct. Right bundle branch block shows an rSR pattern in V1, so the first deflection back from the J point is positive.
D.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 16

D.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: digoxin toxicity, amiodarone toxicity, tricyclic antidepressant toxicity
D.q: A 72-year-old man has amiodarone toxicity. Which actions produce its tracing changes?
opts: Sodium-potassium pump inhibition
Pump inhibition is digoxin's mechanism; amiodarone blocks the ion channels themselves.
Anticholinergic activity alone
Anticholinergic activity is a tricyclic antidepressant effect, causing tachycardia.
Multi-channel and beta blockade
Correct. Amiodarone blocks sodium, potassium and calcium channels and also acts as a beta blocker in the heart, reducing conduction velocity.
An accessory conduction pathway
An accessory pathway is an anatomic bypass (Wolff-Parkinson-White), not a drug action.
D.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 48

D.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
D.q: A 55-year-old woman's monitor shows a regular tachycardia with no P waves. Which QRS finding fits ventricular tachycardia?
opts: Narrow
A narrow QRS means the impulse traveled down the normal conduction pathway from above the ventricles. Ventricular tachycardia is wide.
Not measurable
An unmeasurable QRS is ventricular fibrillation, where there are no organized complexes. Ventricular tachycardia has measurable, wide complexes.
Wide
Correct. The QRS in ventricular tachycardia is wide, because the impulse starts in the ventricle and spreads outside the normal conduction pathway.
Absent
No QRS at all is asystole or ventricular standstill. Ventricular tachycardia produces a QRS with every beat, and it is wide.
D.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 6

D.io: Recognize sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia
D.q: A 12-year-old girl's strip is shown. Which feature separates her rhythm from normal sinus rhythm?
opts: Absent P waves
Sinus arrhythmia keeps a normal P wave before every QRS; only the regularity differs.
A rate over 100 per minute
Over 100 per minute is sinus tachycardia; sinus arrhythmia runs 60 to 100 but irregularly.
A prolonged PR interval
The PR stays normal, 0.12 to 0.20 seconds; what differs is the irregular R to R.
Irregular R to R intervals
Correct. Sinus arrhythmia meets all the sinus criteria (60 to 100 per minute, normal married P waves, normal PR) but its R to R intervals are irregular.
D.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 82, 84
D.alt: Rhythm strip with three-second tick marks and narrow complexes, each preceded by a small upright wave, with gaps that vary in length.

D.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, SVT, atrial tachycardia
D.q: A 67-year-old man's flutter ratio is unclear. How are the flutter waves counted?
opts: Count troughs to the next QRS
Correct. Draw a line through the peaks of the flutter waves and count the troughs until the next QRS complex; that number sets the ratio.
Count QRS complexes for six seconds
That gives the ventricular rate, not the flutter ratio; the ratio comes from counting troughs between QRS complexes.
Measure the PR interval
Flutter has no PR interval, because there are no P waves; count the flutter-wave troughs to the next QRS.
Divide 300 by the boxes
That is the 300 rate method; the flutter ratio comes from counting troughs between QRS complexes.
D.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 26, 27

D.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
D.q: A 63-year-old woman's monitor shows this rhythm. Which feature on the strip gives the rhythm its name?
opts: Identical wide complexes
Identical complexes are the monomorphic form of ventricular tachycardia. Torsades is polymorphic, changing shape as it twists.
P waves without QRS complexes
P waves marching with no QRS complexes are ventricular standstill. This strip is all ventricular activity.
A pacer spike before each QRS
A spike before each wide QRS is a ventricular paced rhythm. There are no pacer spikes here.
Twisting of the points
Correct. Torsades de pointes is French for twisting of the points: the complexes swing from positive to negative around the baseline.
D.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 5
D.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

D.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: left ventricular hypertrophy, right ventricular hypertrophy
D.q: A 66-year-old man with long-standing hypertension has this electrocardiogram. Which finding does it show?
opts: Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy puts more R wave than S wave in V1 and V2. Here V1 and V2 are deep S waves.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Correct. Very deep S waves in V1 and V2 and tall R waves in V5 and V6, adding up well past 35 millimeters: left ventricular hypertrophy.
Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block needs a QRS of 0.12 seconds or longer. The striking change here is voltage, not width.
Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement is a P wave finding. The striking change here is QRS voltage.
D.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 37
D.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

D.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
D.q: A 47-year-old woman's regular strip is shown; consecutive R waves sit four large boxes apart. What is the rate by the 300 method (normal 60 to 100 per minute)?
opts: 75 per minute
Correct. The 300 method divides 300 by the large boxes between consecutive R waves: 300 divided by four is 75 per minute.
60 per minute
Sixty would be five large boxes apart; at four large boxes the rate is 300 divided by four, 75.
100 per minute
One hundred would be three large boxes apart; four large boxes gives 75 per minute.
150 per minute
One hundred fifty would be two large boxes apart; four large boxes gives 75.
D.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 52, 53
D.alt: Lead II rhythm strip on green grid paper with evenly spaced narrow complexes and small tick marks along the bottom.

D.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
D.q: A 72-year-old man's regular strip is shown; his R waves sit about six large boxes apart. What is his rate closest to (normal 60 to 100 per minute)?
opts: About 75 per minute
Seventy-five would be four large boxes apart; six large boxes gives about 50 per minute.
About 100 per minute
One hundred would be three large boxes apart; six large boxes gives about 50.
About 50 per minute
Correct. By the 300 method, 300 divided by six large boxes is 50 per minute (this strip measures about 51), below 60 and so a bradycardia.
About 30 per minute
Thirty would be ten large boxes apart; at six large boxes the rate is about 50 per minute.
D.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 52, 77
D.alt: Rhythm strip with three widely spaced narrow complexes, each preceded by a small upright wave, at equal intervals.

D.io: Review ECG lead placement
D.q: A 63-year-old man's finding appears in two leads that look at the same area. What are such leads called?
opts: Augmented leads
Augmented leads are aVR, aVL and aVF (augmented vector right, left and foot), made from one physical lead; leads viewing one area are contiguous.
Contiguous leads
Correct. Contiguous leads are two or more leads that look at the same area of the heart, such as II, III and aVF (augmented vector foot).
Bipolar leads
Bipolar leads are I, II and III, named for their two poles; leads that view one area are contiguous.
Precordial leads
Precordial leads are the six chest leads; leads looking at the same area are called contiguous.
D.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 70

D.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
D.q: A 55-year-old woman's lead II strip is shown. What pattern do her premature beats follow?
opts: Bigeminy
Bigeminy is a premature beat every other beat; here two normal beats come between each early one.
Quadrigeminy
Quadrigeminy places three normal beats before each early one; here there are two.
Trigeminy
Correct. Every third beat is a premature complex, two normal beats then an early one, repeating: trigeminy.
A triplet
A triplet is three premature beats in a row; here single early beats recur every third beat.
D.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 9
D.alt: Lead II strip with narrow complexes in repeating groups of three, the third of each group arriving early.

D.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
D.q: A 42-year-old man has chest pain and the 12-lead shown. Which region of the heart does the ST elevation localize to?
opts: High lateral wall
The high lateral wall is viewed by I and aVL. On this tracing those leads show ST depression, the reciprocal of the inferior elevation.
Anteroseptal wall
The anteroseptal wall is viewed by V1 to V4. Elevation there would sit in the chest leads, not in II, III and aVF.
Inferior wall
Correct. The ST elevation is in II, III and aVF, contiguous leads that look at the inferior region, so this is documented as an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction.
Posterior wall
No standard lead faces the posterior wall; it shows as isolated ST depression in V1 to V4 and is confirmed with V7 to V9.
D.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 16
D.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

D.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
D.q: A 60-year-old man's rhythm strip is shown at a fast rate. Which usual baseline has disappeared, making ST deviation harder to judge?
opts: The PR interval
The PR interval runs from the start of the P wave to the QRS; it is not the reference baseline for the J point, which is the TP segment.
The TP segment
Correct. The TP segment is the usual baseline for judging the J point, but at fast heart rates it can be hard to locate, and the onset of the QRS is used instead.
The QRS complex
The QRS is still present on every beat; it is the flat TP segment between beats that has disappeared at this rate.
The ST segment
The ST segment is what is being judged, not the baseline it is compared against; that baseline is the TP segment.
D.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 6
D.alt: A single-lead rhythm strip on grid paper at a fast rate

D.io: Recognize common supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation
D.q: A 34-year-old man's rate is 160 per minute (normal 60 to 100); his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no P waves; this tachycardia is perfectly regular with a notch after each QRS.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with P waves of three shapes; this rhythm is regular with one notch after each QRS.
Atrial flutter
Flutter shows a sawtooth of flutter waves between complexes; here only a small notch follows each QRS.
Supraventricular tachycardia
Correct. A regular narrow-complex tachycardia over 150 per minute with retrograde P waves after the QRS (an RP interval rather than a PR) is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia.
D.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 40, 43, 44
D.alt: Gray grid strip with a faint watermark, showing very rapid, evenly spaced narrow complexes with small notches at their ends.

D.io: Correlate ECG findings with clinical implications of ventricular arrhythmias and AV blocks
D.q: A 71-year-old man has second-degree type II block. Compared with type I, how is type II characterized?
opts: More common and more benign
Type II is the rarer and more dangerous of the two second-degree blocks.
Less common but more serious
Correct. Second-degree type II is less common but more serious than type I, and it is always a sign of underlying conduction system disease.
More common and more serious
Type II is more serious, but it is the less common of the two second-degree blocks.
Less common and more benign
Type II is less common, but it is not benign: it is always a sign of disease of the conduction system.
D.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 35

D.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
D.q: A 73-year-old woman has an inferior infarction that also involves her right ventricle. Which artery's occlusion causes this combination?
opts: Right coronary artery
Correct. Inferior infarctions involving the right coronary artery can include the right ventricle, because that artery supplies the right ventricle as well as the bottom of the left ventricle.
Left anterior descending
The left anterior descending artery supplies the front of the left ventricle and septum, not the right ventricle.
Left circumflex artery
The circumflex supplies the side and back of the left ventricle, not the right ventricle.
Left main coronary artery
The left main gives rise to the circumflex and left anterior descending arteries; neither supplies the right ventricle.
D.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 22

D.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
D.q: A 56-year-old man's tracing is described as showing reciprocal changes. What are reciprocal changes?
opts: A second, separate infarction
Reciprocal changes reflect the same event seen from the opposite side, not a second event.
A mirror image on the opposite leads
Correct. Reciprocal changes are the mirror image of a cardiac event on the opposite leads, which look at the same area of the heart from the other side.
Changes seen only after reperfusion
Reciprocal changes appear during the acute event as the mirror image of the elevation; they are not a reperfusion sign.
Artifact from loose electrodes
Reciprocal changes are real physiology, a confirmatory sign of ischemia when ST elevation is present.
D.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 14

D.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
D.q: A 74-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram. Which lateral-lead finding supports the diagnosis?
opts: Notched R waves
Notched lateral R waves without Q waves are the left bundle branch block pattern.
Absent Q waves
Loss of lateral Q waves belongs to left bundle branch block, where the septal fascicle is blocked.
Tall peaked P waves
Tall peaked P waves in the limb leads are right atrial enlargement, not a bundle branch block finding.
Slurred S waves
Correct. Right bundle branch block puts slurred S waves in the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6), the double QRS phenomenon, best seen in V6.
D.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 18
D.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

D.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: Benign Early Repolarization (BER), acute pericarditis, long QT syndrome
D.q: A healthy 25-year-old man's lead V4 is shown. What is the circled notch at the end of the QRS called?
opts: A J wave
Correct. Terminal QRS notching in benign early repolarization is known as the J wave (also the fishhook sign, or Osborn wave).
A delta wave
A delta wave is a slur at the start of the QRS from preexcitation; this notch sits at the end.
A U wave
A U wave follows the T wave and is prominent in hypokalemia; this notch is at the junction of the QRS and ST segment.
A pathologic Q wave
A Q wave is the first negative deflection of the QRS; this is a positive notch at its end.
D.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 7
D.alt: Lead V4 rhythm strip with one area circled in red

D.io: Compare and contrast junctional and idioventricular rhythms
D.q: A 75-year-old man has a regular rhythm at 30 per minute (normal 60 to 100) with no P waves. Which pacemaker is most likely in control?
opts: The atrioventricular node
The atrioventricular node's intrinsic rate is 40 to 60 per minute; 30 is below it, in the Purkinje range.
The sinoatrial node
The sinus node runs 60 to 100 per minute with upright P waves; this is slower and has none.
An atrial focus
An atrial focus would produce P waves; this slow rhythm has none and runs at the Purkinje rate.
The Purkinje network
Correct. A rate of 20 to 40 per minute is the Purkinje network's intrinsic rate, the rate of idioventricular rhythm.
D.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 76

D.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
D.q: A 47-year-old woman has a normal heart. Where is the only place an impulse can pass from her atria to her ventricles?
opts: The bundle of His
Correct. A nonconductive atrioventricular septum separates atria from ventricles, so in a normal heart the bundle of His is the only path.
The atrioventricular septum
The atrioventricular septum is the nonconductive wall that blocks passage; impulses cross only through the bundle of His.
Bachmann's bundle
Bachmann's bundle connects the right and left atria; it does not reach the ventricles.
The coronary sinus
The coronary sinus is a landmark near the atrioventricular node, not a conduction path into the ventricles.
D.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 11, 15

D.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block, third-degree AV block
D.q: A 66-year-old woman's PR interval just before a dropped beat is longer than the PR just after it. Which block is this?
opts: Second-degree type I
Correct. If the PR intervals before and after the dropped beat differ in duration, it is always second-degree type I (Wenckebach).
Second-degree type II (Mobitz II)
Type II has PR intervals of equal duration before and after the dropped beat, because its PR is constant.
Third-degree block
Third-degree block has no consistent PR relationship and no single dropped beat; every P wave is unconducted.
First-degree block
First-degree block never drops a beat. Every P wave is conducted after a long PR.
D.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 50

D.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
D.q: A 46-year-old man's ventricular cell depolarizes in phase 0. Which ion movement produces this upstroke?
opts: Calcium rushing in
Calcium enters in phase 2, the plateau, where it causes contraction; the upstroke is the fast sodium influx.
Potassium leaving
Potassium outflow repolarizes the cell in phases 1 to 3; the phase 0 upstroke is sodium influx.
Chloride rushing in
Chloride is not part of the cardiac action potential as taught here; phase 0 is the rapid influx of sodium.
Sodium rushing in
Correct. In phase 0 fast sodium channels open and a rapid influx of sodium makes the inside of the cell positive.
D.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 19

D.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
D.q: A 35-year-old woman has the wide regular tachycardia shown and does not know whether she has an accessory pathway. How is the correct interpretation made?
opts: Measure the V6 ST-to-T ratio
The V6 ratio separates pericarditis from early repolarization; it cannot tell antidromic reentry from ventricular tachycardia.
Apply Sgarbossa's criteria
Sgarbossa's criteria find an infarction in a left bundle branch block or paced rhythm, not an accessory pathway.
Read the rate from the strip
The rate alone cannot separate the two; at times the difference cannot be told from the tracing at all.
Find delta waves in sinus rhythm

Correct. The tracing alone may not separate antidromic reentry from ventricular tachycardia, which it is treated as until proven otherwise; once cardioversion restores sinus rhythm, a delta wave on that tracing reveals the pathway.
D.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 31; tracing from Slide 33
D.alt: Three-lead rhythm strip on grid paper at a fast rate

D.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement
D.q: A 67-year-old woman has these two complexes, A from lead II and B from V1, with the P wave marked. Which finding do they show?
opts: Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement gives a tall peaked P in lead II and a larger positive first part in V1, the reverse of panel B.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS finding (more R than S wave in V1). These panels mark the P wave.
Left atrial enlargement
Correct. Panel A shows a wide, notched P in lead II, and panel B a P in V1 with a deep negative terminal part: left atrial enlargement.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS voltage finding. These panels mark the P wave.
D.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 30
D.alt: Two drawn complexes labeled A and B, an arrow over the P wave in B

D.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
D.q: A 70-year-old man has this electrocardiogram. What is his electrical axis?
opts: Extreme axis deviation
Correct. Both lead I and aVF are mostly negative: extreme axis deviation, the region called no man's land.
Normal axis
A normal axis has a mostly positive QRS in both lead I and aVF; the normal range is -30 to +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Left axis deviation
Left axis deviation has lead I mostly positive and aVF mostly negative, an axis beyond -30 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation has lead I mostly negative and aVF mostly positive, an axis beyond +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
D.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 26
D.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

D.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
D.q: A 79-year-old man is found pulseless at home, and this is his monitor tracing. What is the rhythm?
opts: Ventricular standstill
Ventricular standstill keeps obvious upright P waves marching across the strip. This tracing has no P waves.
Pulseless electrical activity
Pulseless electrical activity is organized electrical activity with no pulse. This tracing has no complexes at all.
Asystole
Correct. There is no electrical activity, only a wandering baseline: asystole, a lack of electrical activity with no pulse.
Third-degree atrioventricular block
Third-degree block still shows P waves and a slow escape QRS. This tracing has no waves of any kind.
D.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 15
D.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

D.io: Interpret electrocardiographic findings for sinus rhythms: sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
D.q: A 78-year-old man's strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Sinus exit block
Correct. The long gap measures two normal cycles, so the next beat lands on schedule and the P to P intervals march out: the node fired, but one impulse was blocked.
Sinus pause
In a sinus pause the node resets, so the gap is not a whole multiple of the cycle; this gap is two cycles and the beats march out.
Sinus arrest
Sinus arrest misses at least three cycles and resets; here a single cycle drops and the rhythm resumes on time.
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia is evenly slow with no missing cycle; here the spacing is steady except for one dropped cycle.
D.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 85, 89, 90
D.alt: Pink grid strip of narrow complexes with small upright waves before each; one longer flat stretch separates the third and fourth beats.

D.io: Recognize normal sinus rhythm
D.q: A 50-year-old woman's strip is shown. Which feature confirms that the sinoatrial node is the pacemaker?
opts: Narrow QRS complexes
A narrow QRS shows normal ventricular conduction, which junctional rhythms can share; uniform upright P waves show the sinus origin.
A rate under 100
Rate alone does not locate the pacemaker; uniform upright P waves before each QRS identify the sinoatrial node.
Identical upright P waves
Correct. Upright P waves of one shape before every QRS mean the impulse comes from the sinoatrial node; differing shapes point to other atrial sites.
A flat TP segment
The TP segment shows the resting baseline, not the pacemaker; uniform upright P waves show a sinus origin.
D.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 57, 72
D.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip with evenly spaced narrow complexes, each preceded by a small rounded upright wave.

E.io: Topic — Thyroid disorders
E.q: A 61-year-old woman has a slow heart rate and the low-voltage 12-lead shown, with flattened T waves. Which endocrine disorder best fits it?
opts: Hyperthyroidism
Hyperthyroidism is a state of adrenergic hyperactivity; its commonest finding is sinus tachycardia, then atrial fibrillation.
Hypercalcemia
Hypercalcemia shortens the ST segment and QTc; it does not cause global low voltage.
Hypothyroidism
Correct. Hypothyroidism slows the metabolic rate and myocardial contractility: sinus bradycardia with global low-voltage QRS complexes, flattened or inverted T waves, a prolonged QTc and low P waves.
Hyperkalemia
Hyperkalemia peaks the T wave; this tracing's T waves are flattened and its voltage is low.
E.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 45
E.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

E.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular escape rhythms
E.q: An 82-year-old man's strip is shown. What is the wide beat?
opts: A premature ventricular complex
A premature ventricular complex is wide but early; this wide beat comes late, after a long gap.
A ventricular escape complex
Correct. The wide beat comes late, after the point where the next R wave was expected: a ventricular escape complex, as both nodes failed to pace.
A junctional escape beat
A junctional escape beat is late but usually narrow; this late beat is wide.
A premature atrial complex
A premature atrial complex is early and narrow with its own P wave; this beat is late and wide.
E.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 74
E.alt: Strip of narrow complexes with one longer gap, ended by a single broad complex with an opposite-direction wave, then narrow beats resume.

E.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
E.q: A 45-year-old man's rate is 110 per minute (normal 60 to 100); his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Junctional tachycardia
Correct. A regular junctional rhythm with inverted P waves, a short PR and narrow QRS complexes over 100 per minute is junctional tachycardia.
Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia has upright sinus P waves with a normal PR; the short-PR inverted P waves are junctional.
Accelerated junctional rhythm
Accelerated junctional rhythm stops at 100 per minute; over 100 it is junctional tachycardia.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with three P wave shapes; this rhythm is regular with one.
E.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 64, 65, 66
E.alt: Pink grid strip with closely spaced narrow complexes, each followed by a small rounded wave.

E.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
E.q: A 34-year-old man's strip is shown. How is its regularity best described?
opts: Regular
Correct. The same distance separates every pair of consecutive R waves, so the rhythm is regular.
Irregular
An irregular rhythm has unequal R to R intervals; on this strip they are equal throughout.
Regular with one pause
No beat is missing; every R to R interval on this strip is the same.
Irregular when breathing
That describes sinus arrhythmia's varying R to R intervals; here every interval is equal.
E.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 54, 55
E.alt: Rhythm strip with tick marks at the start, middle and end, and narrow complexes spaced at equal distances.

E.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block Type I, second-degree AV block Type II, third-degree AV block
E.q: A 75-year-old man with a history of conduction disease has this strip. What is the rhythm?
opts: Second-degree type I (Wenckebach)
Wenckebach shows progressive PR lengthening before the drop. These PR intervals do not change.
Second-degree type II (Mobitz II)
Correct. A constant PR on the conducted beats with dropped QRS complexes, here with wide QRS complexes, is second-degree type II.
Third-degree (complete) block
Third-degree block has P waves unrelated to the QRS. Here each conducted P wave has the same PR before its QRS.
Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia is a fast, regular wide-complex rhythm with no P waves. This rhythm is slow, with P waves and dropped beats.
E.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 41
E.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

E.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes
E.q: A 68-year-old woman is pulseless. Which finding defines asystole rather than another arrest rhythm?
opts: An organized rhythm with no pulse
Organized activity without a pulse is pulseless electrical activity. Asystole has no electrical activity at all.
P waves with no QRS complexes
Atrial P waves without ventricular complexes are ventricular standstill. Asystole has no P waves either.
Chaotic waves with no QRS
Chaotic waves without measurable complexes are ventricular fibrillation. Asystole has no waves.
No electrical activity at all
Correct. Asystole is a lack of electrical activity, a flat line, with no pulse.
E.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 15

E.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: digoxin toxicity, amiodarone toxicity, tricyclic antidepressant toxicity
E.q: An 86-year-old man taking digoxin develops toxicity although his dose is unchanged. Which explanation does the definition of toxicity allow?
opts: Digoxin blocks the bundle of Kent
The bundle of Kent is the Wolff-Parkinson-White accessory pathway; digoxin toxicity is buildup or oversensitivity.
His heart has become overly sensitive
Correct. Digoxin toxicity occurs when too much digoxin builds up in the body or when the heart becomes overly sensitive to it.
His calcium has fallen too low
Low calcium lengthens the ST segment; it is not the definition of digoxin toxicity.
Toxicity needs a dose increase
Toxicity can occur without a higher dose, when the drug builds up or the heart becomes overly sensitive.
E.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 47

E.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
E.q: A 45-year-old woman has a routine electrocardiogram. What is her electrical axis?
opts: Left axis deviation
Left axis deviation has lead I mostly positive and aVF mostly negative, an axis beyond -30 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Normal axis
Correct. The QRS is mostly positive in both lead I and aVF, so the axis falls in the normal range of -30 to +90 degrees.
Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation has lead I mostly negative and aVF mostly positive, an axis beyond +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Extreme axis deviation
Extreme axis deviation, no man's land, has both lead I and aVF mostly negative. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
E.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 23
E.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

E.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block Type I, second-degree AV block Type II, third-degree AV block
E.q: A 56-year-old man has intermittent dizziness, and this strip is recorded. What is the rhythm?
opts: Second-degree type II (Mobitz II)
Type II keeps a constant PR interval before the dropped beat. Here each PR is longer than the one before.
Second-degree type I (Wenckebach)
Correct. The PR interval lengthens beat to beat until a P wave is not conducted and a QRS drops, then the cycle starts over: Wenckebach.
First-degree atrioventricular block
First-degree block never drops a QRS. This strip has a P wave with no QRS after it.
Third-degree (complete) block
Third-degree block has no PR relationship at all. Here the PR follows a predictable lengthening pattern.
E.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 32
E.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

E.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
E.q: A 69-year-old woman collapses in the waiting room and has no pulse. Her monitor shows this. What is the rhythm?
opts: Torsades de pointes
Torsades has large wide complexes that twist in amplitude around the baseline. This strip has no organized complexes at all.
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia is regular, with identical wide complexes. These waves vary in size and shape with no pattern.
Asystole
Asystole is a flat line, a lack of electrical activity. This strip shows continuous chaotic electrical activity.
Ventricular fibrillation
Correct. Irregular, chaotic waves with no measurable P waves, QRS complexes or T waves are ventricular fibrillation.
E.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 14
E.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

E.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
E.q: A 28-year-old man reviews one cardiac action potential beginning at rest. In what order do the phases run?
opts: The numbers do not run in order from rest: rest is phase 4, which comes before the phase 0 upstroke.
Correct. The cycle starts at rest in phase 4, then the upstroke (0), the notch (1), the plateau (2) and rapid repolarization (3).
Phase 1 follows the upstroke rather than starting the cycle; from rest the order is 4, 0, 1, 2, 3.
Repolarization (3) comes last, not second; from rest the order is 4, 0, 1, 2, 3.
E.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22

E.io: Recognize common supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation
E.q: A 28-year-old woman has sudden palpitations; her rate is 200 per minute (normal 60 to 100). What is the rhythm on her strip?
opts: Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia shows a distinct upright P wave before each QRS; here no separate P wave can be picked out between the complexes.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with P waves of three shapes; this rhythm is perfectly regular.
Supraventricular tachycardia
Correct. A regular, narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves at 150 to 300 per minute is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, commonly called supraventricular tachycardia.
Atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular; these complexes are evenly spaced.
E.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 38, 40, 41, 42
E.alt: Blue grid strip of very rapid, evenly spaced narrow complexes; after each one the trace climbs to a single pointed wave that falls straight into the next complex.

E.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of AV nodal and infranodal conduction abnormalities
E.q: A 76-year-old woman with an atrial pacemaker has a normal-looking QRS after each spike. Why is her QRS normal?
opts: It uses the intact normal conduction pathway
Correct. Atrial pacemakers take over for the sinoatrial node and depend on an intact, properly functioning conduction pathway, so the QRS is normal.
It paces the ventricles directly
Pacing the ventricles directly gives a wide QRS. An atrial pacemaker fires in the atria and lets the normal pathway carry the beat.
It bypasses the atrioventricular node
An atrial pacemaker relies on the atrioventricular node and the rest of the pathway. It does not bypass them.
It fires only after each QRS
The spike comes before the cycle, followed by a normal P-QRS-T. It starts the beat rather than following it.
E.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 18

E.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ventricular hypertrophy
E.q: A 68-year-old man has more R wave than S wave in V1 and V2. Which finding excludes calling it right ventricular hypertrophy?
opts: Right bundle branch block
Correct. Exclusionary criteria for right ventricular hypertrophy are right bundle branch block, posterior wall infarction, and age under 7 or 8.
Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation is a supportive criterion for right ventricular hypertrophy, not an exclusion.
Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement supports right ventricular hypertrophy rather than excluding it.
A strain pattern in V1 and V2
A strain pattern supports right ventricular hypertrophy. Right bundle branch block is the exclusion.
E.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 33

E.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
E.q: A 55-year-old man has chest pain and the 12-lead shown. Which region does the ST elevation in V1 to V3 localize to?
opts: Anteroseptal wall
Correct. V1, V2 and V3 are contiguous leads looking at the anterior and septal walls, so this is an anteroseptal ST-elevation infarction.
Inferior wall
The inferior wall is viewed by II, III and aVF; elevation there would be in the limb leads, not V1 to V3.
High lateral wall
The high lateral wall is viewed by I and aVL; the leads named here, V1 to V3, face the anterior and septal walls instead.
Posterior wall
A posterior infarction shows as ST DEPRESSION in V1 to V4 on the standard tracing; elevation in V1 to V3 faces the anteroseptal wall directly.
E.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 18
E.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

E.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
E.q: A 26-year-old man's 12-lead is shown, with coved ST elevation in V1 and V2. Which structure does his inherited disease affect?
opts: Left ventricular potassium channels
Brugada syndrome is a sodium channel disease of the right ventricular outflow tract.
An accessory atrioventricular pathway
An accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) causes Wolff-Parkinson-White preexcitation, with a short PR and delta wave, not coved V1 to V3 elevation.
The pericardial sac
Pericardial inflammation causes global concave ST elevation with PR depression, not right precordial coved elevation.
Right ventricular outflow sodium channels
Correct. Brugada syndrome is an inherited arrhythmogenic disease that affects the sodium channels of the right ventricle's outflow tract.
E.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 10; tracing from Slide 11
E.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

E.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: COPD/COLD, pulmonary embolism, hypothermia
E.q: An 80-year-old woman with hypothermia has the 12-lead shown. Below which core temperature do these notched waves typically appear?
opts: At about 35°C (95°F) the first change is sinus bradycardia; Osborn waves need cooling below 32°C (90°F).
That is normal body temperature, at which no hypothermic changes occur.
That is a fever. Osborn waves are a hypothermia sign, below 32°C (90°F).
Correct. As the temperature approaches 35°C (95°F) sinus bradycardia appears and the intervals then prolong; below 32°C (90°F) Osborn waves become apparent.
E.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 16; tracing from Slide 17
E.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

E.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement: left atrial enlargement, right atrial enlargement
E.q: A 65-year-old woman's lead II P wave is shown; it measures at least 0.12 seconds (normal under 0.12). What does it indicate?
opts: Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement makes the P wave tall and peaked, over 2.5 millimeters, rather than wide and notched.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS finding in V1 and V2, not a notched P wave.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS voltage finding; the change here is in the P wave.
Left atrial enlargement
Correct. An upright, humped P wave at least 0.12 seconds long with the humps at least 0.04 seconds apart is P mitrale: left atrial enlargement.
E.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 31
E.alt: Drawn tracing of three cardiac cycles

E.io: Apply a systematic approach to ECG interpretation
E.q: A 41-year-old man's P waves are described as married to the QRS complexes. What does married mean?
opts: All P waves look alike
Uniform shape is a separate question (same morphology); married means each P wave is causing its QRS.
Each P wave causes its QRS
Correct. Married P waves are the ones causing the QRS complexes: one P before each QRS, at a constant PR interval.
P waves sit on T waves
A P wave on a T wave would be early and abnormal; married means each P wave causes the QRS after it.
Two P waves per QRS
Two P waves per QRS means some do not conduct; married means one P wave causing each QRS.
E.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 57, 58

E.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: left ventricular hypertrophy, right ventricular hypertrophy
E.q: A 79-year-old man has this electrocardiogram. His R wave in aVL is 22 millimeters (normal 12 or less). Which finding does it show?
opts: Left ventricular hypertrophy
Correct. An R wave in aVL greater than 12 millimeters meets a criterion for left ventricular hypertrophy.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is read from V1 and V2 (more R than S wave), not from a tall R wave in aVL.
Left anterior fascicular block
A fascicular block is an axis and limb-lead pattern with a normal voltage. The criterion met here is aVL voltage.
Right atrial enlargement
Right atrial enlargement is a P wave finding, not an R wave height.
E.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 39
E.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

E.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with bundle branch blocks: right bundle branch block, left bundle branch block
E.q: A 73-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram. Tracing back from the J point in V1, what is the first deflection you reach?
opts: A positive deflection
A positive first deflection back from the J point in V1 is the rule for right bundle branch block. This V1 ends negative.
A flat, isoelectric segment
The QRS in V1 here is a deep negative complex; tracing back from the J point lands on it, not on a flat segment.
A negative deflection
Correct. In left bundle branch block, the first deflection you come to traveling back from the J point in V1 is negative (an rS pattern).
A pacer spike
There are no pacer spikes on this tracing. The first deflection back from the J point in V1 is negative.
E.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 13
E.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

E.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
E.q: A 70-year-old man's strip is shown; two consecutive wide beats are circled. What do they show?
opts: A unifocal couplet
Unifocal premature ventricular complexes share one shape from one focus; the two circled beats look different.
A unifocal triplet
A triplet is three in a row; the circle holds two beats of different shapes.
Ventricular bigeminy
Bigeminy alternates single premature beats with normal ones; here two wide beats come back to back.
A multifocal couplet
Correct. Two premature ventricular complexes in a row make a couplet, and their different shapes mean different ventricular foci: multifocal.
E.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 70, 71
E.alt: Two-lead strip of narrow beats; a circle surrounds two consecutive broad complexes of different shapes.

E.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
E.q: A 59-year-old man's rate is 80 per minute (normal 60 to 100); his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Junctional escape rhythm
A junctional escape rhythm is 40 to 60 per minute; at 80 the junctional rhythm is accelerated.
Accelerated junctional rhythm
Correct. A regular junctional rhythm (inverted P waves, short PR, narrow QRS) at 60 to 100 per minute is an accelerated junctional rhythm.
Junctional tachycardia
Junctional tachycardia is over 100 per minute; 80 falls in the accelerated range.
Normal sinus rhythm
Normal sinus rhythm has upright P waves and a normal PR; inverted P waves with a short PR are junctional.
E.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 59, 60, 61
E.alt: Pink grid strip with regularly spaced narrow complexes, each with a small deflection close in front of it.

E.io: Define: normal axis, left axis deviation, right axis deviation
E.q: A 50-year-old woman asks why her axis is assessed on every 12-lead. Which factors can shift the cardiac axis?
opts: Paper speed and calibration
Paper speed and calibration change how a tracing is drawn, not the direction of the mean electrical vector.
The P wave height and shape
The axis is the direction of the QRS vector. P waves are atrial and do not set it.
The PR interval duration
The PR interval reflects conduction through the atrioventricular node, not the direction of the QRS axis.
Age, history and disease
Correct. A patient's age, medical history and disease processes, chronic or acute, can affect the axis of the heart.
E.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 20

E.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
E.q: A 41-year-old woman has an isolated premature junctional complex on a routine strip. What is its clinical significance?
opts: None, in isolation
Correct. Premature junctional complexes come from increased automaticity of the junction, and isolated ones have no clinical significance.
A run of tachycardia
A single beat is not a run; isolated premature junctional complexes have no clinical significance.
Sinus node failure
A premature beat comes early from increased junctional automaticity; sinus failure produces late escape beats.
Imminent cardiac arrest
Imminent arrest is suggested by a very slow agonal ventricular rhythm; an isolated junctional premature beat is benign.
E.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 50

E.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
E.q: A 55-year-old man has ST elevation in two leads. Which pair counts as contiguous leads?
opts: V1 and aVL
V1 is a septal lead and aVL a lateral one; they look at different walls and are not contiguous.
II and aVL
II is inferior and aVL is high lateral; they look at opposite walls, which makes them reciprocal, not contiguous.
aVF and V1
aVF is inferior and V1 is septal; leads are contiguous when they look at the same region.
II and aVF
Correct. II, III and aVF are contiguous leads that all look at the inferior region, so II and aVF are contiguous.
E.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 16

E.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with supraventricular dysrhythmias: atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, SVT, atrial tachycardia
E.q: A 69-year-old woman's strip shows P waves of three different shapes. What separates multifocal atrial tachycardia from a wandering atrial pacemaker?
opts: Regular R to R intervals
Both are irregular, because the pacemaker site keeps shifting; only the rate separates them.
Absent P waves
Both show P waves of at least three shapes; the difference is a rate over 100 per minute.
Wide QRS complexes
Either may have narrow or wide QRS complexes; the rate over 100 per minute is what separates them.
A rate over 100 per minute
Correct. Multifocal atrial tachycardia is exactly a wandering atrial pacemaker except that the rate is over 100 per minute.
E.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 12, 17, 18

E.io: Interpret electrocardiographic findings for sinus rhythms: sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
E.q: An 81-year-old woman's strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Sinus pause
A sinus pause is a shorter reset gap; once at least three cycles are missed, as here, it is sinus arrest.
Sinus exit block
In exit block the gap is an exact multiple of the cycle and beats march out; this gap does not.
Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus arrhythmia never leaves a long flat gap; it varies the spacing gradually.
Sinus arrest
Correct. The node stops and starts again, and the flat gap spans well over three missed cardiac cycles; the beats after it do not march out.
E.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 95, 99, 100
E.alt: Rhythm strip with four narrow complexes, a long flat baseline several cycles wide, then four more complexes.

E.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of myocardial ischemia and infarction.
E.q: A 66-year-old woman with a recent infarction has this QS complex in V2. What has happened to the tissue under that lead?
opts: It is reversibly ischemic
Reversible ischemia shows as hyperacute T waves or ST depression. Loss of the R wave into a QS complex means the tissue has died.
It has died (infarction)
Correct. A pathological Q wave, here a QS complex with no R wave, represents infarction: the cells beneath that lead have died and can no longer depolarize.
It is injured but alive
Injury (transmural ischemia) is shown by ST elevation. A pathologic Q wave marks the stage after injury, tissue death.
It is normal septal tissue
Normal septal activation produces a small, narrow initial deflection with an R wave following; a deep QS complex after infarction is pathologic.
E.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 12
E.alt: A single electrocardiogram complex on grid paper

E.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
E.q: A 52-year-old woman has this electrocardiogram. What is her electrical axis?
opts: Normal axis
A normal axis has a mostly positive QRS in both lead I and aVF; the normal range is -30 to +90 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Left axis deviation
Left axis deviation has lead I mostly positive and aVF mostly negative, an axis beyond -30 degrees. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Extreme axis deviation
Extreme axis deviation, no man's land, has both lead I and aVF mostly negative. That is not the pattern in leads I and aVF here.
Right axis deviation
Correct. Lead I is mostly negative and aVF mostly positive: right axis deviation, here alongside peaked P waves.
E.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 56
E.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

E.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
