E.q: A 53-year-old woman with chest pain has these precordial T waves but no ST elevation or depression. Why does this finding matter?
opts: It is often the first sign of ischemia
Correct. Hyperacute T waves are often the very first sign of cardiac ischemia. Because there is no ST change to call yet, they are easily missed.
It is a normal variant
Tall, symmetrical T waves in a patient with chest pain are hyperacute, not a variant; normal T waves are asymmetrical and modest.
It proves an old infarction
An old infarction is shown by pathologic Q waves. Hyperacute T waves come at the very start of an ischemic event.
It shows dead myocardial tissue
Tissue death is marked by pathologic Q waves. Hyperacute T waves appear before injury or infarction has developed.
E.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 7
E.alt: Six precordial leads, V1 to V6, on grid paper

E.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of supraventricular arrhythmias
E.q: A 62-year-old man's flutter circuit is mapped. Where does it most often run?
opts: The left atrium
The left atrium can be involved, but flutter's reentry circuit most often runs in the right atrium.
The right atrium
Correct. The reentry circuit of atrial flutter most often occurs in the right atrium.
The atrioventricular node
A reentry circuit over the slow and fast pathways near the node is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia; flutter runs in the right atrium.
The left ventricle
Flutter is an atrial rhythm; its reentry circuit is in the right atrium, not the ventricles.
E.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slide 23

E.io: Recognize sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia
E.q: A 24-year-old woman's monitor shows this strip. What is the rhythm?
opts: Sinus tachycardia
Correct. The rhythm is regular at about 150 per minute (R waves two large boxes apart), with normal P waves married to narrow QRS complexes.
Normal sinus rhythm
Normal sinus rhythm is 60 to 100 per minute; R waves two large boxes apart give 150.
Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus arrhythmia is irregular and 60 to 100 per minute; this strip is regular and fast.
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia is below 60 per minute; this strip runs at about 150.
E.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 78, 80
E.alt: Rhythm strip with closely and evenly spaced narrow complexes, each with a small wave before it.

E.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
E.q: A 27-year-old woman with an accessory pathway has the narrow-complex tachycardia shown. Which route does the circuit take?
opts: Down the accessory, up the normal pathway
That is the antidromic circuit, which depolarizes the ventricles through the accessory pathway and produces a wide tachycardia.
Down the normal pathway, up the accessory
Correct. In orthodromic reentry, conduction toward the ventricles (anterograde) goes through the normal pathway and returns up the accessory pathway, so the QRS stays narrow.
Around the right ventricular outflow tract
The right ventricular outflow tract is the site of Brugada syndrome's sodium-channel disease, not a reentry circuit.
Through the sinoatrial node alone
Reentry needs a circuit: here the normal pathway and the accessory pathway together.
E.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 30; tracing from Slide 32
E.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

E.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
E.q: A 74-year-old woman's right-sided tracing is shown, with ST elevation in V4R during an inferior infarction. Occlusion of which artery explains this?
opts: Left circumflex artery
The circumflex supplies the side and back of the left ventricle. It does not supply the right ventricle that V4R views.
Right coronary artery
Correct. Inferior infarctions involving the right coronary artery can include the right ventricle, which the right coronary artery supplies along with the right atrium.
Left anterior descending
The left anterior descending artery supplies the front of the left ventricle and septum, not the right ventricle.
Left main coronary artery
The left main feeds the circumflex and left anterior descending arteries; the right ventricle is perfused by the right coronary artery.
E.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 22; tracing from Slide 24
E.alt: Electrocardiogram with the V4 label circled and relabeled by hand

E.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrial enlargement
E.q: A 57-year-old man's V1 shows a biphasic P wave with a larger positive first part and a smaller negative second part. What does it indicate?
opts: Left atrial enlargement
Left atrial enlargement is the reverse in V1: a small positive start and a large negative terminal deflection.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy is a QRS finding in V1 and V2, not a biphasic P wave.
Right atrial enlargement
Correct. A biphasic P wave in V1 with a larger positive initial deflection and a smaller negative terminal deflection is right atrial enlargement.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy raises QRS voltage; it does not shape the P wave in V1.
E.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 28

E.io: Correlate ECG findings with clinical implications of ventricular arrhythmias and AV blocks
E.q: A 52-year-old woman had this rhythm and was resuscitated. Which finding on her earlier electrocardiogram would best explain it?
opts: A prolonged QT interval
Correct. The rhythm is torsades de pointes, and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia of this kind is usually a consequence of a prolonged QT interval.
A prolonged PR interval
A PR interval beyond 0.2 seconds is first-degree block, a benign delay in the atrioventricular node that does not lead to torsades.
Grouped beating with dropped beats
Grouped beating is second-degree type I block, a conduction problem in the atrioventricular node, not the setup for torsades.
A pacer spike before each P wave
A spike before each P wave is an atrial pacemaker working normally. It does not explain a twisting ventricular tachycardia.
E.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 11
E.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

E.io: Recognize atrial, junctional, and ventricular premature beats
E.q: A 64-year-old woman's strip is shown. Where do the wide premature beats arise?
opts: In the atria
Atrial premature beats are narrow with an early P wave of new shape; these beats are wide.
In the junction
Junctional beats are usually narrow; these early beats are broad and bizarre.
In the ventricles
Correct. The wide, abnormal early beats with opposite-direction T waves are premature ventricular complexes, here recurring every third beat (trigeminy).
In the sinus node
Sinus beats are the narrow ones with normal P waves; the wide beats come from the ventricles.
E.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 69, 73
E.alt: Strip framed in orange: two narrow beats then one broad beat, repeating across the strip.

E.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
E.q: A 30-year-old woman's tracing could be pericarditis or benign early repolarization. Which lead is used to tell them apart?
opts: aVR
aVR is where pericarditis shows PR ELEVATION; the ST-to-T ratio is measured in V6.
V1
V1 is one of the two leads where reciprocal depression is allowed in both; the ratio is taken in V6.
III
Lead III is an inferior lead; the comparison of ST height with T amplitude uses V6.
V6
Correct. Lead V6 is used: the ST elevation height is compared with the T-wave amplitude in V6, called the lead V6 phenomenon.
E.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 9

E.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
E.q: A 50-year-old woman's ST segment is being examined. Where does the ST segment begin and end?
opts: End of P wave to start of QRS
The end of the P wave to the start of the QRS is the PR segment. The ST segment follows the QRS.
Start of QRS to end of T wave
The start of the QRS to the end of the T wave is the QT interval, which contains the ST segment.
J point to the onset of the T wave
Correct. The ST segment begins at the J point and terminates at the onset of the T wave; in a healthy heart it lies at baseline.
End of T wave to next P wave
The end of the T wave to the next P wave is the TP segment, the baseline used to judge the ST segment.
E.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 5

E.io: Recognize common pacemaker rhythms and pacing artifacts.
E.q: A 78-year-old man has the 12-lead shown. What are the sharp, narrow vertical lines just before each wide QRS?
opts: Pacing spikes
Correct. Each sharp vertical line is the pacemaker's spike, the pacing artifact, followed by the wide QRS it produces in a ventricular paced rhythm.
Delta waves
Delta waves are slurred, gradual upstrokes of the QRS in preexcitation; these are instantaneous vertical spikes.
P waves
P waves are rounded atrial deflections; these are sharp, narrow lines that precede each paced QRS.
Osborn waves
Osborn waves are notches at the end of the QRS, in hypothermia and early repolarization; these lines come before it.
E.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 14
E.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

E.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
E.q: A 48-year-old woman's lead V1 tracing is shown, and its complexes look broad. What duration defines a normal QRS?
opts: 0.12 to 0.20 seconds
That is the normal PR interval; a QRS of 0.12 seconds or more is abnormal ventricular conduction.
Less than 0.04 seconds
That is the limit for a normal Q wave alone; the whole QRS must be under 0.12 seconds.
0.35 to 0.45 seconds
That is roughly the QT interval in males (350 to 450 milliseconds); the QRS must be under 0.12 seconds.
Less than 0.12 seconds
Correct. The QRS duration must be less than 0.12 seconds, under three small boxes.
E.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 31, 60, 61
E.alt: Lead V1 tracing of three beats, each with a broad notched upright complex followed by an inverted wave.

E.io: Compare and contrast sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
E.q: A 66-year-old man has sinus exit block. How do his P waves look when present?
opts: Inverted before each QRS
Inverted P waves point to a junctional origin; the beats in sinus exit block are normal sinus beats.
Of three different shapes
Three P wave shapes describe a wandering atrial pacemaker; exit block beats share one normal sinus P wave.
Replaced by flutter waves
Flutter waves replace P waves in atrial flutter; exit block keeps normal P waves on the beats present.
Normal and married to the QRS
Correct. In sinus exit block, sinus pause and sinus arrest the P waves, when present, are normal and married to the QRS complexes; whole cycles are simply missing.
E.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 86, 92

E.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
E.q: A 60-year-old man needs a posterior tracing. Which electrodes are moved to his back, and what are they relabeled?
opts: V1 to V3, relabeled V7 to V9
V1 to V3 stay on the front; they carry the reciprocal depression. It is V4 to V6 that move to the back.
V4 only, relabeled V4R
Moving V4 alone to the right chest makes V4R, the right-sided lead for the right ventricle, not a posterior tracing.
The limb leads, relabeled V7 to V9
The limb electrodes stay on the limbs. The three lateral chest electrodes are the ones moved to the back.
V4 to V6, relabeled V7 to V9
Correct. To obtain a posterior tracing, leads V4, V5 and V6 are moved to the back of the patient and labeled V7, V8 and V9, and the tracing is repeated.
E.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 19

E.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with atrioventricular blocks: first-degree AV block, second-degree AV block, third-degree AV block
E.q: A 65-year-old man has more P waves than QRS complexes, and his PR interval changes at random from beat to beat. Which block is this?
opts: Second-degree type I
Type I PR intervals are not random: they lengthen progressively in each group until a P wave is not conducted.
Third-degree block
Correct. P waves unrelated to the QRS, so that no PR interval repeats, is third-degree block: the atria and ventricles beat independently.
Second-degree type II
Type II has a constant PR interval on every conducted beat, with some P waves not conducted.
First-degree block
First-degree block has one QRS for every P wave and a long but consistent PR interval.
E.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 42

E.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
E.q: A 29-year-old woman's monitor prints this six-second strip. What is her ventricular rate?
opts: 140 per minute
Correct. Fourteen QRS complexes in six seconds, multiplied by ten, gives a ventricular rate of 140 per minute.
120 per minute
One hundred twenty would be twelve complexes; the strip carries fourteen in six seconds, so 140.
70 per minute
Seventy halves the count; fourteen complexes in six seconds times ten is 140 per minute.
160 per minute
One hundred sixty would need sixteen complexes; fourteen in six seconds gives 140.
E.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 44, 46
E.alt: Six-second rhythm strip with three-second tick marks above and many closely spaced narrow complexes.

E.io: Compare and contrast ECG manifestations of electrolyte abnormalities.
E.q: A 50-year-old woman has a long ST segment and long QTc. Her T wave is checked. What does it look like in hypocalcemia?
opts: Normal in shape and duration
Correct. Hypocalcemia prolongs the ST segment without affecting the duration of the T wave: a long QTc with a normally shaped T wave.
Tall, peaked and symmetric
Tall, peaked, symmetric T waves are hyperkalemia; in hypocalcemia the T wave stays normal.
Flattened with a U wave
A flattened T wave followed by a prominent U wave is hypokalemia; hypocalcemia keeps a normal T wave.
Pushed against the QRS
A T wave pushed against the QRS is hypercalcemia, from a shortened ST segment, the opposite of hypocalcemia.
E.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 40

E.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
E.q: An 81-year-old man with a pacemaker has this strip. Which pacing does it show?
opts: Atrial pacing
Atrial pacing is a spike followed by a normal P-QRS-T cycle with a narrow QRS. These complexes are wide.
Atrial and ventricular pacing
Dual pacing shows a spike before the P wave as well as before the QRS. Here the spike comes only before each QRS.
Ventricular pacing
Correct. A pacer spike precedes every wide QRS, and each T wave points opposite to its QRS: the pacemaker is pacing the ventricle.
Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia has wide complexes but no pacer spikes and a fast rate. Every complex here starts with a spike.
E.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 20
E.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

E.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of AV nodal and infranodal conduction abnormalities
E.q: A 47-year-old man's PR interval is longer than 0.20 seconds (normal 0.12 to 0.20), and every P wave on this strip is conducted. What does this represent?
opts: A block below the atrioventricular node
A block low in the His bundle is second-degree type II, which drops beats. First-degree block is a delay within the node.
Complete atrioventricular dissociation
Complete dissociation is third-degree block, where no P waves are conducted. Here every one is.
A benign delay in the atrioventricular node
Correct. First-degree block is a benign PR interval delay from slowed conduction through the atrioventricular node; every P wave still gets through.
Intermittent failure to conduct
Intermittent failure, with dropped beats, is second-degree block. First-degree block only slows conduction.
E.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 23
E.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip on electrocardiogram paper

E.io: Define: normal axis, left axis deviation, right axis deviation
E.q: A 71-year-old man's QRS is mostly negative in both lead I and aVF. Which axis is this?
opts: Normal axis
A normal axis has a mostly positive QRS in both lead I and aVF; the normal range is -30 to +90 degrees. Here both are negative.
Left axis deviation
Left axis deviation has lead I mostly positive and aVF mostly negative, an axis beyond -30 degrees. Here lead I is negative too.
Extreme axis deviation
Correct. Both lead I and aVF mostly negative is extreme axis deviation, the region called no man's land.
Right axis deviation
Right axis deviation has lead I mostly negative and aVF mostly positive, an axis beyond +90 degrees. Here aVF is negative too.
E.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 26

E.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
E.q: A 60-year-old man is told his left coronary artery divides into two branches soon after it leaves the aorta. Which two?
opts: Circumflex and left anterior descending
Correct. The left coronary artery divides into two branches: the circumflex artery and the left anterior descending artery.
Circumflex and right coronary
The right coronary artery is a separate vessel from the aorta, not a branch of the left; the left divides into the circumflex and the left anterior descending.
Right coronary and left anterior descending
The right coronary artery arises on its own; the left coronary artery's two branches are the left anterior descending and the circumflex.
Coronary veins and coronary sinus
The coronary veins are venous return to the right atrium, not arterial branches; the left coronary artery divides into the circumflex and the left anterior descending.
E.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 4

E.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with dysrhythmias: junctional rhythm, accelerated junctional rhythm, idioventricular rhythm
E.q: A 67-year-old man's rate is 90 per minute (normal 60 to 100); his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Idioventricular rhythm
Idioventricular rhythm is the same wide rhythm at only 20 to 40 per minute; at 90 it is accelerated.
Accelerated junctional rhythm
Accelerated junctional rhythm is usually narrow, with inverted or hidden P waves; these complexes are wide.
Accelerated idioventricular rhythm
Correct. A regular, wide-complex rhythm with no P waves at 40 to 100 per minute is accelerated idioventricular rhythm.
Junctional tachycardia
Junctional tachycardia is a narrow rhythm over 100 per minute; this is a wide rhythm at 90.
E.cite: 12. Ectopy, Escape Rhythms and Supraventricular Dysrhythmias.pptx, Slides 81, 82, 83
E.alt: Gray grid strip with regularly and fairly closely spaced broad complexes and no waves between them.

E.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
E.q: A 41-year-old man's strip is printed at the standard 25 millimeters per second. How long is one small box?
opts: 0.2 seconds
That is one large box, made of five small boxes; a single small box is 0.04 seconds.
0.004 seconds
That is ten times too short; at 25 millimeters per second each 1 millimeter box is 0.04 seconds.
0.04 seconds
Correct. Each small box is 1 millimeter tall and 0.04 seconds (40 milliseconds) wide, not 0.04 milliseconds.
0.4 seconds
That is two large boxes; one small box at standard speed is 0.04 seconds.
E.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 26

E.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: COPD/COLD, pulmonary embolism, hypothermia
E.q: A 47-year-old woman with a pulmonary embolism has new ST-segment and T-wave changes. What causes them?
opts: Pericardial inflammation
Pericardial inflammation gives global concave ST elevation with PR depression, not the embolism's ST-T changes.
Localized myocardial ischemia
Correct. In pulmonary embolism, localized myocardial ischemia leads to specific ST-segment and T-wave changes, alongside tachycardia and a rightward axis.
An accessory pathway
An accessory pathway produces a short PR and delta wave, not ischemic ST-T changes.
Low serum calcium
Low calcium lengthens the ST segment; the embolism's ST-T changes come from localized ischemia.
E.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 50

E.io: Determine the electrical axis of an electrocardiogram
E.q: A 66-year-old man has this electrocardiogram with a narrow QRS. Which conduction abnormality does it show?
opts: Left posterior fascicular block
Left posterior fascicular block gives right axis deviation, lead I negative and aVF positive. Here lead I is positive.
Left anterior fascicular block
Correct. Left axis deviation (lead I up, aVF down), a q wave in lead I with an r wave in lead III, and mostly negative leads II and III with a narrow QRS: left anterior fascicular block.
Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block needs a QRS of 0.12 seconds or longer. This QRS is narrow.
Right bundle branch block
Right bundle branch block needs a wide QRS with an rSR pattern in V1. This QRS is narrow.
E.cite: 14. EKG Axis, BBB.pptx, Slide 7
E.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram

E.io: Review ECG lead placement
E.q: A 58-year-old woman's augmented leads are recorded. What do augmented leads use as their negative pole?
opts: The right leg electrode
The right leg electrode is a ground; augmented leads use the central terminal as their negative pole.
The left shoulder electrode
The left shoulder carries the positive pole of aVL (augmented vector left); the negative pole is the central terminal.
A central terminal in the heart
Correct. Augmented leads use one physical lead and a theoretical negative pole that the machine places in the center of the heart, the central terminal, so they are unipolar.
A chest electrode
Chest electrodes are themselves unipolar leads; the augmented leads' negative pole is the central terminal.
E.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 64

E.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction.
E.q: A 59-year-old woman's tracings are compared over an evolving infarction. Which pairing of finding and process is correct?
opts: ST depression and transmural injury
ST depression represents SUBENDOCARDIAL ischemia. Transmural injury elevates the ST segment.
Q waves and reversible ischemia
Pathologic Q waves represent infarction, the death of tissue, not reversible ischemia.
ST elevation and transmural injury
Correct. ST elevation represents transmural ischemia, also called injury; ST depression is subendocardial ischemia and Q waves are infarction.
Hyperacute T waves and dead tissue
Hyperacute T waves are often the first sign of ischemia; dead tissue is marked by pathologic Q waves.
E.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 12

E.io: Compare and contrast ECG manifestations of electrolyte abnormalities.
E.q: A 71-year-old woman with kidney failure has the 12-lead shown. Which finding on it is the early sign of her electrolyte disturbance?
opts: Flattened P waves
Flattened P waves are a hyperkalemia sign too, but they come later than the peaked T wave.
A wide QRS
QRS widening is a later hyperkalemia change, after the peaked T waves and P-wave flattening.
Peaked T waves
Correct. In hyperkalemia the peaked, symmetric T wave is the early sign; flattened P waves, a wide QRS and finally a sine wave follow as the potassium climbs.
A sine wave
The sine wave is the last and most severe hyperkalemia pattern, not the early sign.
E.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 34; tracing from Slide 35
E.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

E.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with ventricular dysrhythmias: ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, Torsades de Pointes, asystole
E.q: A 58-year-old woman is told her wide-complex tachycardia arises below the atria. Which statement defines ventricular tachycardia?
opts: A tachycardia that originates in the ventricles
Correct. Ventricular tachycardia refers to any tachycardia that originates in the ventricles, monomorphic or polymorphic.
A tachycardia from the atrioventricular node
A rhythm from the atrioventricular node is junctional, not ventricular. Ventricular tachycardia starts in the ventricles themselves.
Chaotic firing of many ventricular foci
Chaotic firing of multiple foci is ventricular fibrillation, which produces no organized complexes and no cardiac output.
A fast sinus rhythm with a wide QRS
A sinus rhythm keeps a P wave before each QRS. Ventricular tachycardia has no P waves, or dissociated ones, because the ventricles drive it.
E.cite: 13. Ventricular Dysrhythmias and Atrioventricular Blocks.pptx, Slide 5

E.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
E.q: A 67-year-old woman's 12-lead is shown, with ST elevation in II, III and aVF. Which leads carry the reciprocal ST depression?
opts: Leads V1 to V3
Isolated depression in V1 to V3 is the mirror of a POSTERIOR infarction. The inferior wall's reciprocal leads are I and aVL.
Leads V5 and V6
V5 and V6 face the lateral wall; on the localization table the inferior wall's reciprocal leads are I and aVL only.
Leads I and aVL
Correct. I and aVL are the reciprocal leads of the inferior wall, and here they show the mirror-image ST depression that confirms the inferior infarction.
Leads II, III and aVF
II, III and aVF are the leads facing the infarct and carry the elevation; reciprocal leads are the opposite ones.
